News.title: Chucky mask-wearing suspect who terrorised city & asked jogger ‘are you ready to die’ after chasing her is unmasked
News.content:
A CREEP wearing a Chucky doll mask who terrorised an entire city and even stalked a female jogger has finally been unmasked.

Chilling footage shows the stalker chasing down a woman on an early morning run in Philadelphia while shouting at her “are you ready to die.”



Cops have launched a manhunt for the suspect who has been identified as Zymire Hughes, 22.

They fear Hughes has fled the state, revealing he has ties to California and Nevada.



They said: “We’re working with the U.S. Marshals to bring him back to face justice.”

An active warrant is out for his arrest.



Shocking footage of the 5.30am incident on August 12 showed the man harassing the female runner.

Philadelphia Police Captain Jason Smith said: “He’s holding his cell phone up in front of her, at which time he asks her ‘Are you ready to die?'”



Smith previously revealed that the jogger injured her leg while fleeing the masked man and was “screaming for help” during the ordeal.

According to police, the suspect made “threatening comments” with his hand behind his back, which caused his victim to “stumble and sustain injury”.

The suspect had allegedly terrorized multiple other people in the community that day, with police claiming he laughed at his victims and similarly asked if they were “ready to die”.



He was reportedly seen filming all of his encounters.

Officers confirmed he would face several serious charges once he’s been successfully apprehended.

Philadelphia DA Larry Krasner said at a news conference on Thursday: “If Zymire Hughes was trying to scare people, make them run.

“Who’s scared now? Who’s running now?’

“You think it’s funny to scare people?



“Well, get ready to get scared by us because we have got the handcuffs. We have got the jail cell.

“We have got the Philly jury that’s going to tell you it’s not funny at all.

“You think it’s funny to make people run, get your sneaks? Because that’s what Zymire Hughes is doing right now.”

DA Krasner divulged that Hughes was on probation for an unspecified crime in Montgomery County.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He continued: “There is nobody in the world who should be trying to imitate what this … man who’s running is doing.



“Now, he’s a punk. I mean, that’s the bottom line. He’s a punk who scared a lot of people for no good reason, and we’re not going to tolerate it.”

News.title: Why did Prince Harry and Prince William fall out? The royal feud explained
News.content:
PRINCE Harry and Meghan Markle’s return to live in the UK and enrol their children into British schools has brought a royal feud back into sharp focus.

While King Charles has welcomed his son following a quiet reunion at Highgrove, royal fans are speculating that Prince William will likely be furious over his brother’s comeback.



What happened?

Once united by the loss of their mother, Princess Diana, the brothers began drifting apart shortly after Harry met Meghan Markle.

Early friction reared its head in 2018 when William reportedly advised Harry not to rush into the relationship, causing Harry to accuse his brother of trying to wreck the romance.



By 2019, after splitting their royal household and joint charity, tensions boiled over during a confrontation at Kensington Palace.

Harry later alleged in his memoir Spare that William called Meghan “difficult”, “rude”, and “abrasive” before knocking him to the floor.



The final breach came in 2020 with “Megxit,” when the Sussexes stepped down as senior working royals following the Sandringham Summit and relocated to California to pursue commercial independence.

In the years following, the rift deepened as the Sussexes released a series of tell-all media projects targeting the Royal Family.

It began with their explosive 2021 Oprah interview, where the couple alleged racism within royal ranks and claimed Meghan was denied mental health support, prompting the late Queen Elizabeth II‘s famous response that “recollections may vary.”

The fallout escalated in 2022 with their multi-million-dollar Netflix docuseries criticising palace operations, which drew widespread backlash over Meghan’s mock curtsy.



By 2023, Harry delivered another blow with his memoir Spare, launching direct attacks on Queen Camilla – labelling her “dangerous” – while exposing intimate details of private rows with William and Princess Kate.

Where the monarchy stands

With the Sussexes soon to be back on UK soil in private accommodation while continuing private business ventures, the Royal Family is divided on how to manage their presence.

King Charles III reportedly remains receptive to the move, keen to spend time with his now UK-based grandchildren and host private family reunions.

In stark contrast, it’s believed that Prince William is firmly opposed, remaining angry over past attacks on Kate and viewing his brother’s return as a major disruption to royal stability.

Meanwhile, key royals like Princess Anne and Duchess Sophie are reportedly approaching the situation with caution, and may reject any “half-in, half-out” hybrid roles that risk commercialising royal status.



Is reconciliation out of reach?

Prince William’s main focus has been supporting Kate through her cancer recovery while carrying the weight of royal duties during King Charles’s own ongoing health battles.

Brits remain divided over the comeback.

Recent YouGov polling revealed just 21% support their return to the UK, while 33% oppose it, and 45% are undecided.

Older generations are particularly resistant, with 57% of over-65s against the move.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Harry continues his work with UK patronages like WellChild and the Invictus Games, but royal experts say a true royal reconciliation may be off the table.



With the brothers living on the same turf once again, avoiding each other will prove difficult, but William’s door is expected to remain firmly shut.

News.title: Ukraine’s daring ‘M&M’ operation to paralyse Moscow airports with 1,000-drone swarm in one night to force Putin to table
News.content:
A UKRAINIAN operation to unleash a swarm of 1,000 drones to paralyse Moscow’s airports in a single night has been revealed.

The plan, code named “M&Ms”, would have stuck the Russian capital in a bid to trap the Russian elite and force the Kremlin into negotiatiations.



Moscow’s four major airports – Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky – were key targets of the mission, two sources familiar with the operation told The Atlantic.

The prolonged disruption would force international carriers to block flights to Moscow, cutting off a key link between Russia’s political elite and the outside world.



If successful, the cunning plot would mark a terrifying milestone in the history of warfare.

A fleet of AI-enabled, low-cost drones were designed especially for the mission.

The UAVs could track down targets using AI guidance systems, without human operators controlling their movements.

Their onboard computers would allow the weapons to compare live camera footage with data stored in their systems.



Once a target was identified, a drone would dive into it and detonate without requiring confirmation from a pilot.

Drone systems like this have been tested by various countries but have never been deployed at scale.

The bombshell plan was developed under former Ukrainian minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

A blueprint was reportedly presented to President Volodymyr Zelensky in early 2026, the sources claim.

The Ukrainian leader raised concerns about the potential risks to civilian aircraft, passengers and airport workers.



But he gave the green light for preparations to continue, according to The Atlantic’s sources.

The plan was then stalled in July following Fedorov’s resignation.

It comes as Kyiv has intensified long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and energy facilities recently.



The crippling strikes have forced Russia – a fuel exporter in peacetime – to import fuel, the government confirmed this week.

And airports across the country were forced to close 114 times between June 28 to July 28 last summer, according to Russian aviation authorities.

The closures were mainly triggered by the threat of Ukrainian drones.

Moscow had the highest number of shutdowns—at least 17 in total at its four main airports.

The Russian capital has been targeted by unrelenting Ukrainian strikes.



Overnight on Tuesday Russian authorities reported that more than 600 drones were heading towards Moscow.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

By Wednesday afternoon Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed more than 1,600 drones had been shot down over a 24-hour period.

A spokesperson for Zelensky declined to comment to The Atlantic.

News.title: Migrant murderer, 59, who committed almost identical knife killing after moving to UK is jailed for life
News.content:
LOCKED UP Migrant murderer, 59, who committed almost identical knife killing after moving to UK is jailed for life

A TWISTED migrant murderer who committed an almost identical knife killing after moving to the UK has been jailed.

Eugeniu Neamtu was found jailed in Romania in 2007 of murdering his housemate Adrian Vas by stabbing him in the chest.



The 59-year-old was freed in 2023 and moved to London where he fatally stabbed flatmate Gheorghe Trica in the chest on February 20 in what a prosecutor said were “strikingly similar” circumstances.

In both cases, Neamtu had rowed with his victims over money and used a similar knife to slaughter his housemates.



He has now been jailed for life with a minimum of 27 years.

Jurors at the Old Bailey were not told Neamtu was previously convicted of murder in Romania after a judge ruled it was too prejudicial.



His grisly past only emerged two days ago when the double killer was found guilty of murdering Gheorghe, 63.

Philip Evans KC, prosecuting, said: “In both cases the defendant was involved in a drunken argument with an associate over money. In both cases he took up a knife from within the home.

“In both cases he stabbed the other man in the chest. In both cases he later claimed that he acted in self‑defence.”

The court heard Neamtu had been drinking plum brandy with Adrian when they rowed over rent and work at their shared home in Romania in August 2006.



He grabbed a knife before stabbing Adrian several times in the chest but claimed he acted in self-defence.

The migrant was jailed for 15 years in Romania then came to Britain as a visitor in September 2023.



He failed to declare his previous conviction or his intention to work to UK authorities and was therefore not in the country lawfully at the time of the killing in 2026.

The court heard Gheorghe was heard shouting “give me back those £5” before he too was stabbed in the chest by Neamtu.

A bystander shouted out: “Oh my God, he has cut Trica”.

Gheorghe was later found collapsed in a pool of blood on a communal balcony outside the front door of the flat.

Neamtu attempted to hide the murder weapon – a black-handled steak knife – by hurling it into a garden.



Detective Inspector Jonathan Potter, who led the investigation, said: “Gheorghe’s death was a tragic and unnecessary loss of life, and our thoughts remain with his family and friends.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Eugeniu Neamtu is a dangerous offender who demonstrated a willingness to use extreme violence during a petty dispute. The jury heard overwhelming evidence of his actions.

“This conviction ensures a dangerous individual has been removed from our communities. We hope today’s verdict offers a sense of justice for Gheorghe Trica’s loved ones.”

News.title: Tragedy as girl, 3, dies after getting trapped in wooden oven playset at babysitter’s home while trying to find her toys
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FOREVER LOVED Tragedy as girl, 3, dies after getting trapped in wooden oven playset at babysitter’s home while trying to find her toys

A TODDLER has suffocated to death after reportedly being wedged inside a wooden toy oven at her babysitter’s home in Florida.

Three-year-old Briella Holmes is said to have become trapped inside the kitchen playset while trying to find toys inside.



Responders were called to a home in the Meadows of Boynton Beach community on July 23.

Fire crews rushed the girl to the hospital in a critical condition but she tragically died four days later.



A babysitter was taking care of Briella along with her sibling when the tragic accident happened.

Boynton Beach police said that the babysitter left the house to go to a shop and left the children in the hands of her partner .



The children were reportedly downstairs playing on their own with the carer occasionally coming down to give them snacks.

On one occasion, the babysitter’s partner came down and saw Briella stuck in the wooden playset.



They freed her and immediately began attempting life-saving measures until first responders arrived, according to cops.

A Palm Beach County Medical Examiner report declared that she died from probable positional asphyxia and ruled her death as an accident.

Positional asphyxia is a type of suffocation where the body’s position prevents one from breathing properly.

Cops said: “This investigation remains active and ongoing.”

“The Boynton Beach Police Department will not be making any additional statements at this time.”



Investigators said that the kitchen playset had been bought second-hand via Facebook Marketplace.

It bore no markings of the brand, manufacturer or model.

A GoFundMe page has said that “Briella was a bright light in the lives of so many.”

“She had a kind heart, a beautiful spirit, and a smile that could light up any room.”

Donations have surpassed their £51,248 target, reaching just over £58,569.

News.title: Sicko who murdered & dismembered girl, 16, laughs as he requests death penalty after admitting luring her to his home
News.content:
EVIL KILLER Sicko who murdered & dismembered girl, 16, laughs as he requests death penalty after admitting luring her to his home

A SICKO laughed in court as he pleaded guilty to torturing and killing a 16-year-old girl he met on a dating app in Florida – and demanded the death penalty.

Steven Gress, 37, walked into a Pinellas County courtroom with a smile on his face before admitting to charges in the killing of Miranda Corsette.



The court heard he felt it was “the right thing to do” – but he maintained that he did not actually kill the victim.

“I did not kill Miranda, but I was involved in certain things that led to her death,” Gress told the judge.



Offering a chilling explanation to his plea, which means that he will receive the death penalty, he said that “life or death is a lose-lose,” the Tampa Bay reported.

Chuckling, the defendant added: “I would rather do the lesser time than spend the next 53 years of my life behind bars.”

Read more about Florida BEACH BLOODSHED Beachgoer pushes pregnant fiancée to safety during ‘bloody’ shark attack



Gress met the teenager on a dating app and lured her to his apartment in St Petersburg on Valentine’s Day last year.

His partner, Michelle Brandes, was waiting for them there.



The pair beat, tortured and sexually assaulted Miranda over the course of a week before eventually killing her over “a stolen ring.”

“This little bi*** stole my ring and won’t give it back, so I’ve been beating her ass,” he told one neighbour who saw the victim at his home, the New York Post reported.

Three other witnesses, including his mother, told the court that Gress had sent them images of Miranda naked, bruised, and in a deteriorating state.



Gress claims that his partner shoved a billiards ball down the girl’s throat and then covered her face with plastic wrap.

He told police when he learned what Brandes did he rushed to poke holes in the plastic to let her breathe, but Miranda had already died.

Gress told the court on Wednesday that he was not fully responsible for her death because she was “free to pull it off her face.”

He said: “I would like to say that I do believe that she killed herself.

“I say that because she had the Saran wrap on her face, but she was free to pull it off her face.”



Police believe Miranda was killed sometime between February 20 and February 24.

Using a chainsaw, Gress then dismembered her body and abandoned it in a dumpster in Hillsborough County, it was alleged.

After entering his guilty plea, he waived his right to a jury trial for the penalty phase of the case.

A pretrial hearing for his penalty phase is scheduled in November.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meanwhile, a pretrial hearing for Brandes will take place in October.

News.title: Warning over school attendance rule that ‘catches separated parents out more than anyone’ ahead of new term
News.content:
SEPARATED parents are being warned over a school attendance rule that could see them landed with a hefty bill this school year.

Anyone found repeatedly breaking the rule could be slapped with a fine of up to £2,500.

As part of its Back-to-School co-parenting report, Mediate UK has reminded parents that attendance fines for unauthorised absences are issued per parent, per child.



This means that if only one parent decides to take children out of school during term time without authorisation from the headteacher, local authorities can fine both parents.



The report reads: “Penalty notices for unauthorised absence in England are issued per parent, per child.

“If one parent takes the children away in term time without the headteacher’s authorisation, the local authority can fine both parents, whether or not the other one agreed to the trip.

“A first notice is £80 per parent, per child if paid within 21 days, rising to £160 after that.



” A second notice for the same child within three years is £160, with no reduced rate.

“After two notices in three years the local authority may prosecute, and a court can impose a fine of up to £2,500.”

The report also details the new branded uniform limit, which has capped the number of compulsory branded items in state-funded schools in England.

The new rules will apply from September 1, and limit branded items of uniform and PE kit to three or fewer.



Secondary schools may require four if one of them is a tie.

News.title: Move over cockapoos – adorable ‘smiley dog’ made famous by Taylor Swift is soaring in popularity, say experts
News.content:
COCKAPOOS may soon be knocked off the top spot as “trendiest dog” – as an unlikely contender could become the nation’s most popular pet.

Taylor Swift’s canine companion has wooed pet lovers with its “smiley” appearance.

Cockapoos have long-reigned as Britain’s beloved designer dog, enticing the nation with their sweet temperament, hypoallergenic fur and adorable “teddy-like” appearance.



But one superstar’s pooch could put an end to all that.



Spotted with a white Samoyed by her side, Taylor Swift‘s newest canine companion could dethrone Cockapoos as the country’s most popular pup.

Pet expert Hedda Båverud Olsson told The Metro: “A single high-profile appearance can shift interest in a breed almost overnight.

“There’s a long history of this, sometimes referred to as the ‘Dalmatian effect’, after Disney’s 101 Dalmatians triggered a surge in demand for the breed decades ago.”



Known for their “sammy smile”, Samoyeds are sought-after for their thick fluffy white fur and friendly, sociable nature, according to Charlotte McNamara, chief canine wellbeing and engagement officer at Royal Kennel Club.

She said: “If Taylor Swift has joined the ranks of Samoyed owners, she’s certainly picked a breed that has won plenty of fans in the UK.”

The dog’s plush coat traditionally served as protection against cold temperatures as it was bred by the Samoyedic people (in Siberia) for herding reindeer, hunting, and hauling sleds.

The pooches gained popularity when Queen Alexandra received one of the first imports in the 19th century, with the Royal Kennel Club (UK) granting the pup recognition in the late 19th century.



Now, Royal Kennel Club figures reveal puppy registrations hit an all-time high in 2022, and have since held steady at around 302 puppies registered each year.

On Instagram, reels of white Samoyeds draw in hundreds of thousands of views, with one account, “melobearthecloud”, having over 28,000 followers.

Meanwhile on Tiktok, Samoyeds Boomer and Diya have 3.3 million followers, and plenty of adoring fans.

So while reputable breeders are unable to scale up demand overnight, the real effect of the pup’s popularity may be visible in just 12 months time.

News.title: El Niño warming set to be 'strongest in living memory', warns Met Office
News.content:
The El NiÃ±o event that is developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest in living memory, the Met Office has warned.

The powerful natural climate phenomenon pushes up global temperatures and can increase the risks of extreme weather.

Added to the effects of human-induced climate change, the Met Office is warning that it is "very likely" to mean 2027 is the hottest year on record globally.

There is growing evidence that weather patterns around the world are already being affected, with below-average monsoon rains in India and suppressed hurricane activity in the Atlantic Ocean.

El NiÃ±o could put the UK at greater risk of a wet, stormy autumn with signs of a very unsettled spell already showing up in long-range forecasts.

"We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event," said Prof Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the UK Met Office.

"I have never seen an El NiÃ±o signal this intense in our forecasts."

There is no clear evidence that climate change is making El NiÃ±o events more likely, but its weather impacts are likely to be more extreme in a warming world.

News.title: Meghan could return to acting once back in UK
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan plan to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence outside London, with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, enrolled to start at school in September.

The decision follows a visit in July by Prince Harry, Meghan and their children to see King Charles III at his Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.

It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.

The BBC understands the King was unaware of the move before last weekend, but he welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.

There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.

Questions have also been raised over whether the Sussexes will receive publicly funded security in Britain. Their UK protection was downgraded after they stopped being working royals in 2020 and moved to the US, where they have paid for their own protection.

Ailsa Anderson, the late Queen's press secretary, said she does not think there will be any plans to give the Duke and Duchess of Sussex official security, adding: "It's a very costly business and they are not working members of the Royal Family."

She told BBC Breakfast that Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the UK was "totally unexpected and fairly astonishing".

But Dai Davies, a former head of royal protection and divisional commander in the Metropolitan Police, said the system for deciding whether someone should receive such protection is "carefully measured".

Davies told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he suspects a review into the Sussexes' security may take place if Prince Harry is to bring his family to the UK and "plans to remain here".

He said that official security is "enormously expensive, especially if you're moving into a premises which is not security prepared".

On Friday, the duke is expected to find out more about how much he, and other high-profile complainants, will have to pay the Daily Mail publisher in costs over a failed legal battle.

The group - which includes Sir Elton John, Baroness Doreen Lawrence and Elizabeth Hurley - sued Associated Newspapers Limited over claims of unlawful information gathering, but last month all their claims were dismissed.

News.title: My life was changed by a terror attack - now survivors like me won't be forgotten
News.content:
Travis Frain was texting his mates a photo he had just taken of Big Ben on a university trip to London when his day turned from normal to anything but.

"One of the guys in my group shouted 'look out' and as I looked up from my phone the terrorist's car was in front of me.

"It was a split second really before the car hit me. I went over the bonnet, into the air, before landing back on the ground."

This was 22 March 2017, when attacker Khalid Masood drove his car into crowds, killing four, before stabbing a police officer to death outside Parliament.

Frain, then 19, was left with multiple injuries including a fractured leg, which took two years to heal. "There will always be a part of you affected by that attack."

Now 28, he spoke to BBC News as the UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism is set to take place on Friday.

News.title: Stifling heat and broken toilets: TUI River Cruise passengers tell of their holiday hell
News.content:
Dozens of people have accused TUI River Cruises of operating vessels with faulty facilities including persistently broken air conditioning, after they spent thousands of pounds on holidays.

Earlier this year passengers on the Skyla, a ship operated by TUI, contacted BBC Your Voice to say they had been stranded in Budapest during a heatwave with little to no air conditioning.

Following that report more people got in touch to say they faced similar problems on both the Skyla and its sister vessel, the Isla. They criticised TUI's customer service and said the refunds offered were inadequate.

TUI apologised to customers where trips "fell short of the standards we aim to deliver".

A spokesperson for TUI, said: "We understand the disappointment and frustration caused to affected customers."

Passengers described stifling conditions as well as problems with plumbing after paying thousands of pounds for European cruises, including on the Danube River.

Andy Peach and his wife booked a seven-day trip on the Skyla in June, travelling through Budapest, Vienna and Linz.

It turned out to be "the worst TUI holiday we've ever been on", he said.

Instead of air conditioning, Peach said there were "big blowers" on board, expelling hot air.

"One was in the middle of the corridor, blocking the exit," he said. "It didn't seem to cool the place down."

Temperatures onboard climbed as the holiday went on leaving him "exhausted", he said. By the end of the week, Peach said the air conditioning in cabins had broken too.

On the second-to-last day passengers were transferred to hotels, which Peach said were "really basic".

He and his wife had paid nearly Â£4,000 for the holiday but they were offered only Â£300 as a refund and given 72-hours to accept it.

He said: "TUI know there's problems on these boats, but continue to sell them to people as a full luxury cruise."

News.title: Steve Rosenberg: Shortage of petrol but not patriotism as Russians feel growing impact of war
News.content:
At a petrol station in the south-east of Moscow, Svyatoslav has been queuing in his car for two hours.

The sign board up ahead has just been changed to show there's no fuel.

"They say there will be petrol here," Svyatoslav tells me optimistically. "They just don't know when. Maybe today, maybe tomorrow."

I ask him why he doesn't drive off and look for another place to fill up.

"I haven't got enough in the tank to do that," Svyatoslav replies.

Even if he had, there'd be no quick fuel fix for Svyatoslav. This week across Moscow, and in other parts of Russia, there have been long queues for petrol.

"Unscheduled repairs at oil refineries," explain Russian officials.

Those repairs have been triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. Such long-range attacks sparked major fuel shortages earlier this summer. The targeting of oil refineries has continued apace.

This time the queues in Moscow are even longer than before. The authorities appear to be struggling to resolve problems with refining capacity and logistics.

"The second wave of the fuel crisis is building," declared broadsheet Nezavisimaya Gazeta this week.

Driving around Moscow this week two things catch the eye: patriotic announcements on giant billboards about Russian Flag Dayâ¦and giant petrol queues.

Outside one Moscow petrol station I count 80 vehicles waiting in line.

The search for fuel is now a constant struggle.

"Last night I went to get petrol at 11pm," says Elizaveta who's queuing again for fuel. "By midnight I'd reached the front of the queue. Then they shut the petrol station until 2am."

"I drove into Moscow yesterday from the provinces," says Lyubov. "It was empty petrol stations all the way."

News.title: The town whose council wants migrants to move in
News.content:
A new shop opened along Greenock's fading High Street in May. Anik African Store has brought a small corner of Nigeria to the Scottish town, selling yams, plantain, okra and catfish.

It is not the only African food shop here - there is another just metres away, responding to the area's changing population.

Five years ago, locals say, it would have been rare to see a black person in Greenock. Now hundreds of Africans and refugees have moved to the area.

The local council has in fact come up with a plan to attract even more to this corner of the west of Scotland as a means of stemming its falling population.

Scottish people "are lovely and accommodating", says Anik's owner, Christianah Omilana, who came to the UK in 2021. "Immigrants will come when there is work", she adds.

News.title: French becoming more effective in stopping small boat crossings, UK says
News.content:
French police tactics are becoming more effective in stopping small boats in the English Channel from reaching Britain, the Home Office has said.

It credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.

Footage released by French police shows officers racing across a beach in jeeps to intercept a launch. Once the boat is abandoned, an officer slashes it lengthways with a knife.

The Conservatives described the announcement as a "joke" and said Channel crossing preventions were "down by half over the past year".

Migrants can be seen throwing objects at the officers, one of whom appears to respond with pepper spray.

While Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, thousands of illegal migrants are getting through with 250 arriving on Monday.

In late July a record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat with Border Security Command pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on 23 July.

The Home Office, citing French police figures, said that since it struck a deal with France three months ago which included additional funding for authorities, 61% of small boats have been intercepted - a five per cent increase compared to last year.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the "UK-France deal is already having a real impact".

The UK-France Border Security deal agreed in April under the Starmer government, includes Â£501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and Â£161m for new approaches.

Previously the French authorities allowed most dinghies to head towards the UK once they had launched, because of the risk of intercepting them in deep water, while loaded with people.

Of the 12 dinghies stopped so far at sea, three interceptions took place in the last two weeks.

The techniques being used have not been disclosed by the UK or France.

Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at the Border Security Command, told the BBC that "last Thursday alone, the French prevented all three of the boats that tried to cross".

Speaking to the BBC at the Western Jetfoil facility in Dover used to process migrants, he said: "Two of those they prevented at sea, and one they prevented on land."

News.title: UK borrows more than expected in July as Healey prepares for first Budget
News.content:
The government borrowed more than expected in July, according to figures published as Chancellor John Healey draws up his first Budget.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said borrowing, the gap between what the government spends and what it collects in tax, was Â£1.8bn during the month.

Official forecasters had expected a surplus of Â£500m, meaning the government borrowed Â£2.3bn more than predicted.

Economists warned the figure will restrict Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham's room for manoeuvre as they target measures aimed at easing the cost of living for households, with little room to increase borrowing in the Budget on 27 October.

Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" at the Budget â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

He has adopted his predecessor Rachel Reeves' fiscal rules, which commit the government to funding all day-to-day spending through tax receipts by the end of the decade.

Responding to the borrowing figures, Healey said: "We are cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 economy, while giving people a bit of breathing space with cost of living pressures and focusing support to get young people into work."

July's borrowing figure was significantly lower than June's Â£16bn, with a surge in self-assessed income tax receipts boosting the government's coffers for the month. But economists said the public finances would come under renewed pressure when the one-off lift, typical for July each year, runs out.

Despite falling from June to July, the borrowing figure was higher than expected. Experts pointed to increased welfare spending, including benefits and other payments such the state pension, with social payments coming in Â£2bn higher than the same period last year.

The ONS said borrowing from April to July, the first four months of the government's fiscal year, has reached Â£56.7bn. This is lower than last year, but Â£2.3bn higher than forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which the government uses when drawing up its spending plans.

News.title: Will Harry's return heal deep-rooted rift with William?
News.content:
This isn't a regular sibling fallout. It is a deep-rooted fracture filled with anger, resentment and a total loss of trust.

And much of it has played out in public.

The Prince of Wales remains in no mood to forgive and forget. The hurt he feels lingers.

"William is very stubborn," a family friend told the BBC. "To feel cheated by your own brother has been painful. He can't just put it behind him."

But in his interview with the BBC last year, Harry offered a different view.

"I would love reconciliation with my family. There's no point in continuing to fight any more."

The problem for Prince William now is proximity. Harry will be in the UK within two weeks, probably a short drive away from Windsor where William's family lives.

There will be pressure on the elder brother to take the lead, ease the pain and just make up with Harry now the siblings will be living in the same country.

"I think William doesn't care about the pressure to reconcile," said royal author, Valentine Low. "If he doesn't want to reconcile with his brother because of the things he's done, the wrongs that he feels Harry's done to him, he's not going to reconcile. But it does improve the chances I think."

Former editor of The Sun and presenter of the When it Hits the Fan podcast David Yelland said: "This is one of the biggest news stories in the world: the schism between William and Harry. Until these two brother get together or show us there is a rapprochement that story is going to make it very difficult."

He told BBC Breakfast: "Every single thing they do, where ever William goes, he will be asked about this because Harry is back in the neighbourhood.

"We don't need cuddles, we don't need posed-up photos, we just need a briefing that they have met. This is a real PR crisis for the Royal Family. William has to reach out, if he doesn't we are going to be talking about this every day for years and it's going to become a reputational threat."

The Prince of Wales will prioritise his public work in the coming months and try not to get drawn into the drama around the UK return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Several people from organisations who have worked with Prince William told BBC News of their desire to support William and help avoid Harry and Meghan becoming a distraction.

One source, who has worked on charity projects with the Royal Family, described wanting to protect the future King.

"This is a hard situation for him full of emotion and anger and we will support him," the source said. "It is really important for me to ensure that any work we do with William will be focused on making a positive change and won't be affected by the Harry and Meghan drama."

News.title: Man denies charge over Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
A man has denied failing to disclose information in relation to the Manchester synagogue attack.

Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim appeared before Westminster Magistrates' Court and pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity.

The 49-year-old, of St James Road in Higher Broughton, Salford, spoke only to confirm his name and indicate his plea. He was remanded into custody to appear at at the Old Bailey on 25 September.

Worshippers Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October.

He then began attacking with a knife, while wearing a fake suicide belt, before being shot dead by police outside the synagogue.

News.title: Rain to stop in time for weekend as sun returns
News.content:
High pressure is set to build across the UK over the next few days bringing drier weather for the weekend.

Heavy downpours have brought rain to parts in need this week - albeit with some flash flooding - but these are set to ease.

Many areas will see sunny spells across Saturday and Sunday with daytime temperatures climbing again, perhaps to above the August average in parts of the south of England.

However the nights will turn rather chilly.

News.title: Search for cruise ship passenger feared to have fallen overboard
News.content:
A major search has been launched after a passenger was reported missing from a cruise ship docked in Dundee.

Lifeboats and coastguard crews are searching for the man who is feared to have fallen from the Ambassador Ambition before it arrived in the city on Friday.

It is understood that the passenger's luggage was still onboard and his bed had not been slept in.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said the man's next of kin had been made aware and inquiries were ongoing.

One passenger told BBC Scotland News that tannoy announcements had repeatedly called the name of a specific passenger during the morning.

The alarm was raised onboard the ship at about 08:35 on Friday, about 36 nautical miles from Arbroath.

They were then told a passenger was missing.

News.title: Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs
News.content:
Royal Mail has once again missed its delivery targets for first and second class post, but said it is making progress towards the goals as its turnaround plan continues.

The postal service delivered 85% of first class deliveries the next day between March and June, up from 76% in the same three months of 2025, but below regulator Ofcom's 90% target.

Second class mail was delivered within three days 91% of the time, another improvement from the previous year, but short of Ofcom's 95% target.

Royal Mail said the results are "encouraging and show that the work we are doing to improve the service is having an impact".

Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services (IDS), has struggled with rising competition in the delivery market, fewer people sending letters and fines from the regulator for missing targets in recent years.

But it said that, compared with the same period last year, the portion of first class mail delivered next-day had risen significantly while the amount of second class mail delivered within three days had improved slightly.

Chief operating officer Jamie Stephenson said: "These results are encouraging and show that the work we are doing to improve the service is having an impact.

"First Class performance is well ahead of where we expected to be at this stage of our Improvement Plan, while Second Class is tracking in line with the plan."

Stephenson added that there is "more to do", pointing to a Â£500m investment plan to improve the firm over the next five years. The plan includes a commitment to meet Ofcom's delivery targets by May 2027.

The postal service has faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over the slowness of its letter delivery.

It is currently under investigation by Ofcom for the second year running for failure to meet its delivery targets.

The regulator fined it a record Â£21m in October last year for missing targets in 2024-25.

In March, postal workers from across the UK told the BBC they were being asked to move or hide mail from senior bosses so it looks like delivery targets were being met.

The firm apologised to Gloucester residents where post was sometimes delayed for months, admitting its service there was "totally unacceptable".

Most recently, people in Worcestershire hit out over postal delays, complaining of weeks-long delays for important post to arrive, with some missing hospital appointments.

Royal Mail recently said it aims to meet regulator Ofcom's targets by May 2027 as part of a turnaround plan costing around Â£500m in the next five years.

"We know there is more to do," Stephenson wrote in a statement. "We are investing Â£500 million over five years and making significant changes across our network... None of this progress would be possible without the continued hard work of our frontline colleagues, including through the recent extreme heat."

IDS was bought in 2025 by Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky.

News.title: Killer jailed for murdering second flatmate
News.content:
A man has been jailed for life for murdering his flatmate in the UK just three years after completing a prison sentence in Romania for a "strikingly similar" killing.

Construction worker Eugeniu Neamtu, 59, known as Jimmy, was found guilty of fatally stabbing his flatmate Gheorghe Trica, 63, in Walthamstow, east London, on 20 February.

Appearing at the Old Bailey on Friday, Mr Justice Marks sentenced Neamtu to life with a minimum term of 27 years.

Neamtu had stabbed his fellow Romanian Trica in the heart in almost identical circumstances to an earlier killing in his home country dating back to 2006, the court heard.

In May 2007, he was jailed for 15 years in Romania for murdering his housemate by stabbing him repeatedly in the chest in a drunken row over money.

News.title: World's oldest person celebrates turning 117
News.content:
The world's oldest living person celebrates turning 117 years old in Surrey on Friday with her family and friends.

Ethel Caterham, who lives at Hallmark Lakeview Care Home in Lightwater, took on the mantle in April 2025 after the death of Brazilian nun Sister Inah Canabarro Lucas at the age of 116.

Born three years before the Titanic disaster and eight years before the Russian Revolution, Ethel has also lived through two world wars.

In addition, she is one of the oldest people to survive Covid-19, after contracting it in 2020 at the age of 110, according to Guinness World Records.

Originally from Shipton Bellinger in Hampshire, the second youngest of eight children, Ethel was raised in Tidworth, Wiltshire.

The last surviving subject of King Edward VII, as a teenager she travelled to India in 1927 and began working as an au pair to a military family there.

News.title: Starmer donates biography of himself to Downing Street library
News.content:
A book about the life of Sir Keir Starmer has become the newest addition to the Downing Street library, after being donated by Sir Keir himself.

Keir Starmer: The Biography, written by journalist and former Labour adviser Tom Baldwin, has now joined the collection of more than 400 books, some of which are kept in two bookcases in Downing Street's Cabinet Room.

The library was established in 1931 by the first Labour Prime Minister, Ramsay MacDonald, and since then prime ministers and ministers have been invited to make contributions.

Seven ministers who served in Sir Keir's government have also added books to the shelves.

The new donations include:

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves added her own book, Alice in Westminster: The political life of Alice Bacon

Darren Jones, who served as a senior minister between 2024 and 2026, gave Laudato Si: On Care for our Common Home - a book by Pope Francis which calls for greater protection of the environment

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy offered her book All In: How we build a country that works

Nick Thomas-Symonds, a Cabinet Office minister in the last government, also chose his own book - a biography of former Labour Prime Minister Harold Wilson

Women and Equalities minister Bridget Phillipson picked Choose Freedom: The Future for Democratic Socialism by former Labour deputy leader Roy Hattersley

Former Wales Secretary Jo Stevens gave The Fed: a history of the South Wales miners in the twentieth century by Hywel Francis and Davis Smith

Treasury minister James Murray donated Instruction to Deliver - a book by Sir Michael Barber about his experience being a civil servant in Tony Blair's government

As Labour leader, Sir Keir did not appear to be much of a reader. In one interview in 2024, he struggled, external to name a favourite novel and when he appeared on Radio 4's Desert Island Discs he picked an atlas as the book he would take with him.

In contrast, his successor Andy Burnham, an English Literature graduate, has spoken of his fondness for poetry, in particular the works of Tony Harrison and Philip Larkin.

He is unlikely to donate a volume to the library at this early stage of his premiership, but if he finds time to peruse the shelves, he will find an eclectic collection.

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has claimed that the club will “definitely sign some players” before the end of the summer transfer window, with the Spaniard admitting his squad is “still quite thin” in places.

The departures of Mohamed Salah, Ibrahima Konate and Curtis Jones – as well as a long-term injury to Hugo Ekitike – mean that the Reds are light in some key areas as the 2026/27 season begins.

Winger Victor Munoz and defender Ronaldo Araujo have been the only arrivals this summer, though Jeremey Jacquet has also arrived at Anfield after a £55m deal was agreed for the Frenchman back in February.

Andoni Iraola is trying to bring high-intensity football back to Anfield ( PA )

And Iraola addressed the need for more arrivals before the end of the window, with the former Bournemouth manager explaining that some deals take longer to complete. “We will definitely sign some players. Some deals you have to wait until the end,” Iraola told Sky Sports.

“But the end is the important picture, the one we will have on September 1, because it is true that we are still quite thin,” added the Spaniard.

While there is plenty of talent in the Reds’ squad, more depth – and some quality in key areas of the starting XI – will be needed if they are hoping to challenge for the Premier League title.

The club has been actively pursuing reinforcements, most notably on the wings, and Iraola may well have been referencing a deal for PSG winger Bradley Barcola when he pointed out how some deals take longer than others.

The Reds have held an interest in the Frenchman since the beginning of the summer, and while they have been negotiating with PSG, the two clubs remain apart in terms of valuations, with the European champions reportedly demanding £145m for the Frenchman.

Liverpool also had a recent bid of £50m turned down for Brighton winger Yankuba Minteh, though it is not known whether they will re-visit a move for the Gambia winger.

The Reds kick off their 2026/27 campaign away to Newcastle, with that game taking place on Sunday, 23 August at St James’ Park.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has claimed more than 2,500 lives and is expanding exponentially across a region larger than France, a senior official has warned.

Speaking via video call from Bunia, a city in the north-eastern part of the country, senior United Nations Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis issued an urgent plea for additional funding, warning that current financial reserves will be depleted within weeks.

The crisis is being compounded by local hostility towards medical staff, as well as responders falling ill and dying from the infection.

This 17th Ebola epidemic became the largest in the country's history by case numbers in late July, eclipsing the previous worst outbreak that lasted from 2018 to 2020. It is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which no approved treatments or vaccines exist.

"The Ebola outbreak is growing exponentially," Harneis said.

open image in gallery More than 2,500 people have died and health workers have faced attacks ( AP )

"The epidemic is spreading to an area that is bigger than France, and the outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response. And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs."

Roughly 160 healthcare workers have contracted Ebola during the crisis, resulting in 43 deaths.

"And then, when we do respond, apart from the threat from the virus, healthcare workers and frontline workers have been attacked by youths, ambulances have been burned and stoned, and the healthcare facilities have been attacked," Harneis stated.

"Fear translates into angry young men who start throwing stones at their object of fear, the ambulance," he added.

Aid workers report that local communities have fallen prey to conspiracy theories claiming the virus is a hoax, while strict health protocols preventing families from personally burying loved ones have fuelled further resentment.

More than 260 incidents targeting health workers have been recorded over the last six months, leaving eight dead, Harneis said, "which is obviously terrifying because people are already risking their lives to deal with Ebola."

Furthermore, international aid cuts in recent years have curtailed humanitarian capacity. Operations have also been hampered by difficulties paying tens of thousands of response personnel, as government restrictions on commercial flights disrupted the delivery of physical cash to local banking services.

Thames Water has said its hosepipe ban is likely to be enforced until the end of the year.

More than 27m people across England have now had hosepipe use restricted in their area, including Thames Water’s 10.1m customers after a ban was put in place last month.

After several heatwaves over a record-breaking summer and historic lows of rainfall, hosepipe restrictions in England’s capital and surrounding areas could last for several months, the water firm said.

Nevil Muncaster, strategic water resources director at Thames Water, told Times Radio: “I think realistically, it’s going to be towards the end of the year before that comes off.

Millions of people in the UK are under hosepipe bans ( PA Archive )

“That’s something that we need to make sure we do just to protect the environment.”

Earlier this week, it urged customers to continue efforts to reduce water use as it revealed household demand has fallen by 3 per cent across London and more than 6 per cent across the Thames Valley and Home Counties since a hosepipe ban began on 23 July.

In an update on Tuesday, the utility said London reservoir storage was at 74 per cent, which is lower than what the firm would expect for this time of year but the Farmoor Reservoir in Oxfordshire is 92 per cent full.

It also said rainfall in the Thames catchment area during July was less than 1mm, which is just 2 per cent of the long-term average, while customers used around 100 million litres more water every day than normal, adding further pressure to rivers, reservoirs and the water network.

Mr Muncaster said that dry conditions were still expected, even though some rain is forecast to fall.

“The Environment Agency forecast is that it will be drier than normal for the next few months, but we’ll wait and see,” he added.

The beleaguered water firm, which is the country’s largest, is struggling under almost £20bn in debt, with cash running out to see the firm through beyond the end of this year and widespread concern about which direction is best for the future of the business.

Mr Muncaster told Times Radio that a new reservoir at Abingdon in Oxfordshire is unlikely to be ready until 2040.

He also defended the fact the company’s £250m Beckton desalination plant, which opened in 2010 to provide water during droughts, had been offline this summer.

He said: “It was something we planned. We had a very wet winter, so we took the opportunity to do that maintenance, expecting us to be able to work through the summer.”

The world’s oldest person is set to celebrate her 117th birthday on Friday after a year of “many firsts”.

Ethel Caterham became the oldest living person in April 2025 after the death of Brazilian nun Sister Inah Canabarro Lucas at 116.

Soon after, she shared her simple yet profound secret to a long life: avoid arguments. "Never arguing with anyone, I listen, and I do what I like," she said.

Mrs Caterham, who lives at Hallmark Lakeview Care Home in Lightwater, Surrey, will spend her special day with her family and friends.

In a statement, she said: “Thank you for all of the kind birthday wishes. Even at 117, I’ve had many firsts this year, from stroking a llama to holding hands with the King.

“I’ve had a lovely day celebrating with my family and friends, and I look forward to seeing what next year brings.”

open image in gallery King Charles III met Ethel Caterham at Hallmark Lakeview Care Home ( PA )

Mrs Caterham was visited by Charles, who held her hand as he introduced himself, in September last year, just after her 116th birthday.

During the meeting with Charles, she recollected his 1969 investiture as the Prince of Wales when he was 21, adding: “All the girls were in love with you and wanted to marry you.”

Mrs Caterham was born on August 21, 1909, in Shipton Bellinger, Hampshire, five years before the start of the First World War, as the second youngest of eight siblings.

She is the last surviving subject of Edward VII, who died in May 1910.

In 1927, aged 18, she travelled to India and worked as an au pair to a military family until she was 21.

open image in gallery Mrs Caterham lives in Surrey ( Hallmark Luxury Care Homes )

She met her husband Norman, who was a lieutenant colonel in the British Army and died in 1976, at a dinner party in the UK in 1931.

They lived in Salisbury before being stationed in Gibraltar and Hong Kong. Mrs Caterham set up a nursery school while in Hong Kong and raised two daughters, both of whom died before her.

One of her sisters, Gladys, lived to be 104.

Mrs Caterham drove until she was 97 and enjoyed playing contract bridge in her centenarian years. She also survived Covid-19 in 2020, aged 110.

The title of the oldest person ever is held by French woman Jeanne Calment, who lived to 122 years and 164 days, according to Guinness World Records.

Heavy downpours returning to drought-stricken regions across the UK carry a risk of flash flooding, forecasters at the Met Office have warned.

The warning follows a period of heavier rain on Wednesday and Thursday, coming after a summer marked by severe heatwaves and dry weather. These conditions have left the whole of Wales and nearly three-quarters of England in drought.

Data from the Environment Agency (EA) indicates that the northwest of England experienced the wettest weather over the past 24 hours, with 52.5mm of rain recorded in the Lancashire seaside town of Morecambe.

This single volume represents a third of the region’s average overall rainfall logged between 1 June and 18 August this year, which reached up to 156mm, according to the Met Office.

Significant rainfall also fell across southern parts of the country, where an EA monitoring station at Pevensey Bay in East Sussex registered 32mm of rain over the same 24-hour period.

“Most parts of the UK have seen at least a few splashes of rain, but many parts have seen a little bit more than that,” Craig Snell, senior meteorologist at the Met Office, said.

open image in gallery Further showers are forecast on Friday for most parts of the UK, although they are not likely to be as widespread or heavy as they were on Thursday ( PA )

“Generally, it’s been a big change in the last 24 to 48 hours compared to what many parts of the UK have seen in the last couple of months.”

But the wetter conditions, which come after the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, also create a risk of flooding as heavy showers fall on baked dry ground, Mr Snell warned.

“Unfortunately, some of these showers which have fallen have caused some impacts.

“Parts of the North West have seen some localised flooding, and also parts of the south coast of England over the last 24 hours or so.

“Part of that is down to the fact that the rain is falling on quite baked ground, so the water is not sinking in like it would usually do.”

Showers continued near coasts on Thursday evening, but will likely fade away across inland areas overnight, with clear spells developing elsewhere, according to the Met Office.

Further showers are forecast on Friday for most parts of the UK, although they are not likely to be as widespread or heavy as they were on Thursday for many, Mr Snell said.

Some thunderstorms are also likely overnight across parts of Wales and western England, Mr Snell said.

open image in gallery People shelter under umbrellas from the rain in Whitehall, central London ( PA )

Drier and sunnier conditions are expected to return over the weekend, although temperatures will remain in the low 20s in the southern parts of the country, and in the high teens to low 20s in the north.

“Tuesday onwards, we are likely to then see some further rain,” Mr Snell added.

“Most, again, probably in the form of showers moving in from the South West.”

A drought response expert group has also warned of the risk of flooding because of heavy showers, with the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) adding drought conditions continue to worsen despite the recent rainfall.

The National Drought Group – which includes the Met Office, Government, regulators, water companies, farmers, Canal & River Trust, anglers, and conservation experts – has moved to weekly meetings as part of their drought response, a spokesperson for Defra said on Thursday.

Many areas of the country are facing water shortages as reservoir levels have fallen to 62.6 per cent – 16.3 per cent lower than is expected for this time of year, according to Defra.

Last week, a £65 million package was also announced to support farmers, whom Defra said have reported their earliest harvest in 20 years, with yields impacted by heat stress and dry weather conditions.

EA chief executive Philip Duffy, who chairs the National Drought Group, said: “This summer has been extremely challenging for farmers and for wildlife, and the rain we have seen this week is desperately needed.

“This current rainfall isn’t enough to change the overall drought picture, and it is possible to have simultaneous drought and flood as heavy rain falls on compacted soils.

“We are monitoring the flood risks, while also working with industry, agriculture and the government on the ongoing drought response.

“In the meantime, we really do need everyone’s help to make our current water reserves last.

“Every drop saved is an extra drop for your local river, lake or farmer.”

open image in gallery A heavy rain shower stops play during the Rothesay County Championship Division 1 match between Warwickshire and Sussex at Edgbaston ( Getty )

The Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales have also applied to the English and Welsh governments for a drought order for the River Severn, warning of the impact the conditions are having on the Severn’s habitats and surrounding farmers.

If granted, it would require Severn Trent Water, South Staffordshire Water, Bristol Water and Hafren Dyfrdwy to reduce the amount they abstract from the river by 5 per cent, which they have said will not affect water supplies.

Dr Katie Facer-Childs, senior hydrologist at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, said: “After this exceptionally hot and dry summer, it will take several months for river flows and reservoirs to get back to normal.

“A little rain will not end the drought.

“Autumn and winter is a crucial period for replenishing our water resources.

“If this autumn is wetter than normal, river flows may recover by December, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely and river flows will therefore generally remain low into the new year, especially in the South East.

“A dry winter could leave parts of the UK vulnerable to drought again next year.”

News.title: 12 best Korean skincare products, tested by a beauty writer
News.content:
Korean skincare has become a global phenomenon. Making a ritual out of daily skin routines, the Korean skin care philosophy focuses on hydration, barrier support, and preventing signs of aging and environmental damage. And many of us are re-thinking our skincare cabinets because of it.

Innovation-led and with the use of targeted ingredients, such as fermented extracts, centella asiatica, and advanced UV filters, Korean skincare products often stand out against Western counterparts. They can also be the better option when it comes to affordability, too.

The use of targeted ingredients, such as fermented extracts, centella asiatica, and advanced UV filters, often makes these products stand out against Western counterparts. And they sometimes come at a more affordable price point.

With the recent launch of South Korean beauty megastore Olive Young in the U.S., buying K-beauty online has never been easier. News.title: Congo gambles on ‘old’ vaccine as new Ebola virus spirals
News.content:
Nearly half of all those infected have gone on to die.

Dr Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine partnership, earlier this week said to beat the outbreak “we must deploy every tool at our disposal”.

She went on: “To avoid this becoming the worst recorded Ebola outbreak in history, it is critical that all effective countermeasure options are brought to bear.

“We have a tool that could help save lives while we wait for [Bundibugyo]-specific vaccines to become available.”

Previous clinical trials have shown that Ervebo is safe, but its effect on other strains is unknown.

The World Health Organisation said in a statement that while it was not known if Ervebo may protect against the Bundibugyo virus, “early laboratory and animal data suggest it may provide some protection”.

Medics told the Telegraph of anecdotal claims that health workers who had been given Ervebo to protect them during an outbreak of the Zaire strain in 2018 to 2020 had not fallen ill during the current Bundibugyo outbreak.

Health workers are at extreme risk of catching the disease because they come into contact with highly-contagious blood, vomit and diarrhoea from dying patients. When they fall sick themselves, they frequently go on to infect their own families.

Giving health workers vaccine jabs to protect them as they tend the sick is a cornerstone of Ebola responses.

The WHO said the vaccine allocation includes 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus. The remaining 50,000 doses will be used for front-line and health workers as recommended by WHO experts.

Dr Nishtar said: “Having already been licensed for the Zaire strain, we know that Ervebo is proven to be safe.

“And while the signs are that it may not stop transmission – which is essential for ending the outbreak - it could well save precious lives and reduce suffering.”

Health officials warn that the Bundibugyo outbreak centred on DRC’s Ituri province is easily outpacing relief efforts.

The virus is thought to have been spreading for months before an outbreak was finally declared in mid-May and medics have been unable to make up the head start.

An analysis by the Africa Centres for Disease Control meanwhile warned the current outbreak dwarfed all others on record

The current outbreak had almost ten times more cases than any other previous outbreak at a similar stage.

News.title: Soaring welfare bill pushes national debt to almost £3tn
News.content:
Britain’s soaring welfare bill forced John Healey to borrow more to balance the books last month.

The gap between tax receipts and spending unexpectedly resulted in a £1.8bn deficit in July, taking the national debt to within a whisker of £3tn.

Economists had predicted the Government would borrow nothing and blamed the deficit on the rising welfare bill.

Figures published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) this morning show total debt rose to £2.985tn in July.

Benefit payments also climbed by 7.2pc, or £2bn, to £30bn last month.

The Chancellor now faces another tax-raising Budget in October, even as strong receipts from self-employed workers provide some respite.

The ONS also said Mr Healey spent £7.7bn on debt interest in July alone, almost 10pc higher than a year ago.

Ashley Webb, at Capital Economics said: “The weak performance was mainly due higher social payments.”

Monthly borrowing was slightly higher than the Office for Budget Responsibility and markets expected, meaning the Government has borrowed £56.7bn this financial year to plug the gap between tax receipts and public spending.

Julian Jessop, an independent economist and IEA economics fellow, said: “The latest official data highlight the fragility of the public finances as John Healey prepares his first Budget. Government borrowing was £2.3bn above forecast in July, and £0.7bn higher than in the same month a year ago.”

July is traditionally a strong month for receipts from the self-employed, with self-assessed income tax receipts last month coming to £17.1bn, about £1.7bn more than a year earlier.

However, higher inflation triggered by the Iran war means Mr Healey will be forced to use the Budget to find billions of pounds to repair the public finances.

Mr Healey said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of our UK economic stability and national security which is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules, with a buffer against global uncertainties.”

The Resolution Foundation warned that the Chancellor’s headroom against his fiscal rules - self-imposed guardrails to guide public spending - has shrunk from around £24bn in the Spring Statement to less than £8bn today.

The think tank called on the Chancellor to use his first Budget on Oct 28 to put the nation’s finances on a more sustainable path.

Elliott Christensen, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said: “The Chancellor’s margin against his fiscal rules is now razor thin.”

News.title: Brook falls agonisingly short of Headingley hundred again as England continue to dominate
News.content:
“Yeah, of course I did,” said Cox, when asked if he was frustrated to miss out on three figures. Cox was caught behind off spinner Ali Usman, but believed he had hit his pad with his bat, not the ball.

“Once I got to fifty, I moved to sixty quickly, and thought ‘there’s a chance here’. Just keep being disciplined, ball by ball. I had it at the back of my mind, thinking you have worked so hard, do not give this opportunity up. That is exactly what I do in county cricket. I get to fifty, see how many runs I need to score, and work down from there.”

Asked if his team-mates were feeling the same emotion, he said: “Oh yeah there is. Every team, every player wants to score Test hundreds. Four of us got fifties, so we were hoping one would kick on, and instead of making it just a hundred, make it 150 or 170.

“I am thrilled. I would have taken it at the start of the Test match. I let myself down a tiny bit, but at the end of the day, you take 70.”

Cox resumed on day two on 23, then was dropped by the bowler Khurram Shahzad on 57. In the course of his innings, he was compared to AB de Villiers by the former England captain Michael Vaughan.

Cox is likely to get a good run across formats. England had hoped to call on Sam Curran for the third Test of this series, but his summer is over due to a groin injury. Curran will undergo surgery on Friday.

It is likely England will be without Curran, Bethell and Tom Banton for September’s white-ball series against Sri Lanka, which should mean greater opportunity for the likes of Cox and Sussex’s James Coles, and could even see a recall for Zak Crawley, who made an assured 81 for Kent against Middlesex on Thursday. Will Jacks is currently sidelined with appendicitis, but is expected to have recovered in time for the series.

He also has that edge, the grunt of an angry fast bowler, and his competitiveness was just what Root needed considering his other quicks were still in Hundred mode. News.title: Burnham blames Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation
News.content:
Andy Burnham has blamed Donald Trump’s war in Iran for higher inflation in Britain.

Inflation jumped from 2.6pc in June to 2.9pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics, threatening to undermine Mr Burnham’s pledge to bring down the cost of living.

The Prime Minister said: “We can’t control though what is going on in the Middle East and the effect of the conflict there is now being felt in inflation here, and in other countries around the world.

“I realise these times are really hard but already people can see a month into office I have done things that will make a difference.”

July’s inflation figure was affected by a 13.5pc rise in the Ofgem price cap in response to the energy crisis unleashed by the Iran war. It means prices are now rising at their highest rate since March.

The latest figure shows the struggle that Mr Burnham faces to fulfil his promise to bring down living costs.

There are fears that inflation will climb higher in the coming months as the impact of the conflict filters through to the economy.

Speaking at an event in the North East, Mr Burnham added: “I want to lead a cost-of-living Government, and I’ve already taken steps as Prime Minister to show I will help people wherever I can. I can’t do everything, I think people know that.

“We’re in tough times, but where I can do something to make life that little bit better, I will do it.”

Since arriving in No 10, Mr Burnham has made tackling the cost of living a key policy focus.

The Prime Minister announced last month that he would remove VAT from electricity bills from October and reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares from next year.

However, average energy bills are expected to jump by around 4pc from October, according to energy analysts Cornwall Insight, wiping out any potential savings from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

The analysts said Ofgem’s price cap – which limits the average annual energy bill faced by a family home – would rise from £1,663 to £1,729.

Despite concerns about increasing gas and electricity bills, July’s rate of inflation was in line with economists’ expectations.

Money markets now expect policymakers at the Bank of England to hold interest rates at 3.75pc at their next meeting in September.

Sports.title: I faced Cristiano Ronaldo in 2004, now I’m still going strong at my 22nd club aged 45 and even played with my two sons
Sports.content:
TWO exciting young forwards faced off when Manchester United beat Northampton Town in the FA Cup fourth round in January 2004.

More than 22 years on, Cristiano Ronaldo and Derek Asamoah are both still going strong.





Ronaldo is a fledgling 41 compared to 45-year-young Asamoah, who is showing no signs of slowing down – quite literally.

The veteran scored just 70 seconds into his Whitstable Town debut in the FA Cup extra preliminary round a fortnight ago to become one of the competition’s oldest scorers.

Dream Team is back, free, and there’s £100,000 up for grabs!

His new Kent side face Newhaven on Saturday for a spot in the first qualifying round.

Revealing his secrets to his incredible longevity, Asamoah told SunSport: “There was a lot of hype around the Northampton-United game between Ronaldo and me because we both like doing skills and entertaining the crowd.

“It was a really good battle.

“It’s absolutely crazy we are both still playing.





“Age is just a barrier.

“I’m proud I’m not just a bit-time player making up numbers for the fairytale.

CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

“I’m playing 90 minutes, contributing goals, leading the team. I’m still one of the quickest.

“I’ve always really looked after myself.

“I’ve done my stretches, prepared properly and don’t just jump out of bed and put my boots on.

“I rest right. I eat really clean. I go to the gym regularly. I’m not a drinker. After games, everyone sees me with water.

“Sometimes, I play Saturday and Sunday.”

Ninth-tier Whitstable are the 22nd club of Asamoah’s ultimate journeyman career, which began aged 17 in 1999 at Barking – a whopping 27 years ago.

He spent much of the noughties in the Football League before a complicated transfer to Ligue 1’s Nice, followed by spells in Scotland, Bulgaria and South Korea, returning to England with Carlisle in 2014.



Impressively, he can rattle off his full CV in order.

Derek Asamoah's amazing career 1999: Barking 1999: Asante Kotoko 2000: Hampton & Richmond Borough 2000–2001: Slough Town 2001–2004: Northampton Town 2004–2005: Mansfield Town 2005–2006: Lincoln City 2006: Chester City (loan) 2006–2007: Shrewsbury Town 2007–2009: Nice 2009: Hamilton Academical 2009–2010: Lokomotiv Sofia 2011–2012: Pohang Steelers 2013: Daegu FC 2014–2016: Carlisle United 2016–2017: Carlisle United 2017: Guiseley 2017–2018: Haringey Borough 2020: Cheshunt 2021–2023: New Salamis 2023–2024: Brightlingsea Regent 2024: New Salamis 2024–2025: Haringey Borough 2025–2026: Sittingbourne 2026–present: Whitstable Town 2004-2011: Ghana

Asamoah, who manages properties around his football, earned four caps for Ghana alongside Michael Essien and Asamoah Gyan.

But midway through his fifth decade, he has no plans to retire, especially after memorable family moments.

Asamoah explained: “Every year since I turned 39, I’ve told myself I’ll quit if I don’t score 20 goals in a season. Since then, I’ve scored 150 goals.

“People who’ve retired say they knew when it was time.

“Right now, the love of the game keeps me going and my body feels in top-notch condition.

“I’m probably the only player who hasn’t seen the physio in ages. I don’t get any massages, taping or strapping.



“Cheshunt signed both me and my son Maleace. We made our debuts together and also played for New Salamis together.

“In one game, we both scored and he assisted me.

“I played with my son Zayshaun at Haringey and Sittingbourne, where we both scored in a game and I assisted his winner.

“Some people have kickabouts with their kids in the park. I feel so blessed by what we’ve achieved. It’s unbelievable. “

Speaking of unbelievable, on-loan Shamrock Rovers forward Maleace is reportedly the fastest footballer in the world.

Asamoah Sr added: “Maleace actually recorded the fastest time in football at 40kmh (24.8mph) for Wigan.



“Kylian Mbappe’s at about 39km. I don’t think anyone’s broken Maleace’s record.

“But I keep telling him that in my prime, I’d have beaten him. I managed 35kmh last year.”

For comparison, the top speed clocked at the 2026 World Cup was Mbappe’s 37.6kmh.

Asamoah is motivated to keep playing for another decade for another son.

He revealed: “My six-year-old Ezra said to me, ‘Dad, are you going to be playing in ten years because I want to play with you as well?’

“I told him I’ll try my best to hang on, but can’t promise.”



Asamoah has been scoring goals for nearly 30 years. So has he stuck with one celebration throughout or constantly created new moves?

He concluded: “I’m a simple guy. It’s a little fist bump. The only time I went overboard was when Carlisle played Liverpool at Anfield.

“I told my team-mate beforehand I had a celebration I wanted to do.

“He set me up for my goal, I did the cartwheel, got on my knee and shot him. The way he went down was beautiful. It was like a Hollywood movie.”

Even by Hollywood’s standards, Asamoah’s script is a never-ending blockbuster.

The France and Chelsea legend was a key part of Chelsea’s success in the 2000’s, winning two Premier League titles, an FA Cup and two league cups.



But now he thinks Todd Boehly and the Chelsea ownership are ‘surfing’ on the foundations laid by those before him, which sends a “terrible message” to the fans.

He thinks Chelsea need to have an established first team for young players to develop into, and that the new ownership are not building that.

Makelele said: “Chelsea has always developed players, always produced young talent, but always on one condition: before the kids come through, there has to be something to come through into.

“A talented, competitive first team, where youth is blended with great players. That’s Chelsea’s DNA, and that’s what the club needs.



“The new owners have their own projects, of course.

“But you cannot simply take what we built at Chelsea and surf on it. That sends a terrible message to the fans, to the people who love this club. And we’ve seen the results: out of the Big Four, struggling in Europe, humiliated at times.

“It’s frustrating, and it’s not the Chelsea we know.”

As it happens, chairman Boehly and investment partner Walter are said to be in talks with majority shareholders Clearlake Capital over a deal to offload their combined holdings in Chelsea – which account for more than a quarter of the business.

And while things have been messy at Stamford Bridge since BlueCo took charge, there seems to finally be some hope in south west London this season, having appointed Xabi Alonso as manager and with no European football to worry about.

He added: “This is the Premier League. This is not the Bundesliga, where Bayern dominate everything and three or four teams trail behind.
