Sports.title: Uefa and Concacaf discuss joint Nations League in latest challenge to Fifa
Sports.content:
Uefa and Concacaf have begun talks about setting up a combined Nations League tournament featuring all 96 European and North and Central American and Caribbean countries, in another direct challenge to Fifa.

The Guardian has learned that having come together to push for Gianni Infantino’s removal in the light of the World Cup sell-off controversy, the two confederations are now working on creating their own biennial tournament, which could launch as early as 2028 after the next European Championship.

Although discussions are at an early stage, it is understood the new competition would mirror the current multi-league format used for the existing Nations Leagues by Europe’s governing body and Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football. It would be followed by a knockout phase, a final-four tournament to determine the champions.

League A would feature the top teams in Europe, including Spain, France, England and Germany, playing competitive league fixtures against the highest-ranked nations in Concacaf such as Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Uefa and Concacaf launched Nations League competitions in 2018, with the confederations staging fixtures in the same international windows, so the mechanics required to set up a joint tournament are already in place.

Under the draft plans the league phase would be played during the existing September, October and November international breaks, followed by knockout matches in March and finals in June.

As the fixtures would take place during international windows that have already been agreed, it is unclear whether the new tournament would need to be ratified by Fifa, although given the world governing body is in the midst of an existential crisis with Infantino facing a leadership challenge that may be a moot point.

With serious discussions having begun only in the last few weeks, the number of teams in each league has yet to be determined, but all 96 members of Uefa and Concacaf would be involved and much of the revenue pooled, generating significant additional income for smaller nations.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino is under pressure with Uefa and Concacaf pushing for his removal and now planning a combined Nations League tournament. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

The commercial appeal of the bigger European teams playing regular competitive matches in North America and Canada would be considerable, while there would also be major benefits for Mexico, whose football federation (FMF) is known to be frustrated by what it sees as the financial limitations of playing within Concacaf.

The FMF has held initial discussions about leaving to join the South American confederation, Conmebol, in a move that would need to be ratified by Fifa, but the prospect of lucrative matches against European opposition could lead to a change of heart.

The proposed new format would replace rather than add to existing international fixtures, while games would be played in geographic blocks to reduce travel.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is also understood to have expressed interest in joining a global Nations League at a future date, and the competition structure being discussed would be flexible enough to accommodate them. The AFC does not currently operate a Nations League, however, so that would be a more long-term aspiration.

Uefa and Concacaf have been working together for some time, and signed a memorandum of understanding to promote greater cooperation at Fifa’s congress in Vancouver in April, but have become even more closely aligned since the World Cup sell-off plan emerged last month.

Both confederations have made it abundantly clear that they regard Infantino’s position as untenable as a result of his role in the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, and are working together to propose an alternative candidate to stand against him in the presidential election next March.

Uefa declined to comment, although one source with knowledge of the proposal confirmed discussions are under way.

Concacaf declined to comment directly, but highlighted the confederation’s longstanding commitment to collaboration, which has led to guest teams participating in the Concacaf Gold Cup.

A historically strong relationship with Conmebol has resulted in many South American teams taking part in the Gold Cup, as have South Africa, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

Sports.title: Tottenham close on deals for Manchester City’s Savinho and Omar Marmoush
Sports.content:
Manchester City are close to agreeing the transfer of Savinho to Tottenham for £85m, with a separate deal of around £75m for the arrival of Omar Marmoush from the FA Cup-winners to the north London club also being worked on.

Savinho signed for the City Football Group in summer 2022 for 40m euros (£30.8m), first joining Troyes, so the prospective sale of the 22-year-old for £85m represents a near £55m profit for City’s owners. After loans at PSV and Girona, the Brazilian joined City two years ago but the winger failed to establish himself as a first-choice under Pep Guardiola, the former manager.

Marmoush was bought in January 2025 for around £59m but, as with Savinho, the Egyptian forward was not a regular starter under Guardiola, due to having to compete with Erling Haaland.

If Spurs do buy both Savinho and Marmoush, that would take the club’s investment in Roberto De Zerbi’s squad this summer to £387m, after the purchases of Sandro Tonali for £100m, Mateus Fernandes (£85m), and Jan Paul van Hencke (£52m).

Sports.title: PSG are the best team in Europe. The rest of Ligue 1 are just trying to survive
Sports.content:
On the eve of a new Ligue 1 season, many clubs seem a little distracted. Even those accustomed to competing at the top have concerns that transcend the pitch. In a league that contains the greatest team on the continent, the focus of the majority of clubs has shifted to surviving and providing, rather than competing.

Any fighting spirit has long since been kicked out of Paris Saint-Germain’s competitors; back-to-back Champions League titles will do that. It feels like a long time ago since Kylian Mbappé moved to Real Madrid on a free transfer, leaving behind a scent of opportunity that filled the nostrils of Marseille, Monaco and Lille. Roberto De Zerbi was bullish when he joined Marseille. “I’m not here to finish second,” said the manager, who has since moved to Tottenham. Finishing second has now become an aspiration, especially for a club such as Marseille, given their predicament.

Of all of the distracted teams, Marseille are the most preoccupied with off-field matters. While the club avoided a European ban, allowing them to compete in the Europa League this season, Uefa’s tone was one of a final warning: redress the financial imbalance or you’re out.

There has been a change in the dugout, with the (almost boringly) dependable Bruno Génésio coming in for Habib Beye, who replaced De Zerbi in February, but the demands made by Uefa – and the DNCG, French football’s financial watchdog – have prevented the club from making a single signing. There have been plenty of sales (Mason Greenwood, Facundo Medina, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang and Gérnoimo Rulli have all left on permanent deals), but not enough for Marseille to contemplate dipping into the market themselves.

Marseille’s “everything must go” sale suggested the club were in survival mode and their reaction to Pierre-Emile Højbjerg refusing a move to Newcastle confirmed it. He was stripped of the captaincy for the club’s friendly against Atlético Madrid. Génésio said it was a decision made above his station and one he disagreed with. “I am an employee. I have to agree to certain obligations,” he said.

View image in fullscreen Pierre-Emile Højbjerg was stripped of the captaincy for Marseille’s friendly against Atlético Madrid. Photograph: Icon Sport/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

Génésio wants to keep Højbjerg, but the austerity cure ensures the club are hell-bent on doing the opposite. It is a situation that perfectly encapsulates the conflict between sporting ambition and financial necessity, familiar to many clubs in Ligue 1, and increasingly those competing towards the top of it – lest we forget Lyon’s recent brush with administration.

With the authorities “supervising their wage bill”, Monaco have made savings this summer. Maghnes Akliouche’s £43m move to PSG has been programmed for some time, and Folarin Balogun and Lamine Camara may still bring in big fees before the end of the window. The unexpected sale of Aladji Bamba to Newcastle for £34m has given the club more breathing room in their quest to cut costs and raise funds.

TV broadcasting rights are no longer the lifeblood of Ligue 1. Instead, French clubs rely on the reckless abandon of Premier League sides making multimillion-pound bets on unproven young players. Bamba had played 18 league games when Newcastle came with the big money. Ligue 1 has always been a ​stopover for its top talents, but the rate of churn has hit new levels. Liverpool did not wait around before signing Jérémy Jacquet and Mamadou Sangaré only needed one campaign at Lens to convince Brentford he was worth an expensive bet.

Even those in stronger financial health cannot resist advances. The prospect of coaching Lens in the Champions League could not prevent Pierre Sage from crossing the Channel to join Crystal Palace. Sangaré made a similar journey, while Adrien Thomasson, Malang Sarr, Allan Saint-Maximin and Wesley Saïd – all instrumental in Lens’ second-place finish and maiden Coupe de France triumph last season – have been lured away. Success can be a poisoned chalice. At least their rebuild, under Dino Toppmöller, looks intelligent. You’d expect nothing less from Lens, but their pillaging once again exposes the limits to success in Ligue 1 for clubs that do not go by the name PSG.

View image in fullscreen Allan Saint-Maximin celebrates after scoring for Lens in the Coupe de France semi-final against Toulouse. He has now moved to MLS. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters

The reigning champions, who are in search of a sixth consecutive league title, have often been accused of being distracted by the Champions League. When you win it two years in a row, you can justify it, but after their close race with Lens last season it isn’t an accusation that can be levelled at them this summer. Their starting XI is already the best in the league and beyond, so PSG’s transfer guru, Luís Campos, has focused on improving the second string that more often than not will be trotted out in Ligue 1.

Ferran Torres, Akliouche and Mika Godts are upgrades on the departing trio of Gonçalo Ramos, Lee Kang-in and Randal Kolo Muani, even if they will struggle to dislodge the current starters in the PSG attack. Lucas Digne is a shrewd pick as back-up to Nuno Mendes, too.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

PSG will probably have an easier ride in the league this season as the teams chasing them have either regressed or stagnated. Rennes, who must this season contend with European football for the first time in three seasons, are the only side that finished in the top seven last season that – on paper – look stronger than they were at the start of the summer.

Wealth immunises Rennes, to a degree, but Strasbourg are weaker after losing important players to Chelsea. Emanuel Emegha, the club captain, has been followed out the door by Valentín Barco, with the goalkeeper Mike Penders returning to his parent club after a loan spell at the Meinau. The latter has been replaced by Filip Jörgensen, who will have to play a “crucial role”, in the words of their new manager, Hugo Oliveira, formerly assistant to Marco Silva at Fulham. Time will tell if Jörgensen is up to the task; he was surplus to requirements at Stamford Bridge so it may be a move born out of convenience. In any case, he will be busy if pre-season is anything to go by; Strasbourg have conceded 21 goals in their seven friendlies.

The managerial upheaval, from Liam Rosenior to Gary O’Neil, and now to Oliveira, also contributes to a feeling of instability at Strasbourg, one of 10 clubs part of a multi-club model in Ligue 1 this season. That, in itself, adds a feeling of “Who is this even for?” to the upcoming season. Not all clubs in these models are subservient, but nor do their own interests always guide decisions.

Rosenior knows all about that. The new Paris FC manager is one of two coaches returning to France in search of redemption following failed stints in England, with the former Southampton head coach Will Still joining Auxerre. There are also some more adventurous appointments, in the form of Davide Ancelotti at Lille and Filipe Luís at Monaco. There have been an incredible 12 managerial changes in France’s top flight for this season: plenty of change, even if some things will almost certainly stay the same.

This is an article by Get French Football News

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Endrick to Liverpool? Arsenal to swap Martinelli for Yildiz?
Sports.content:
After Vinícius Júnior signed a shiny new deal at Real Madrid, Arsenal are having to look elsewhere for a new winger. Turkey’s Kenan Yildizm who plies his trade with Juventus, is of interest to Mikel Arteta and the Gunners hierarchy. One potential way of getting the deal done is to send Gabriel Martinelli in the opposite direction.

It is all fun and games at Manchester City where they are trying to rebuild a midfield inside a week. Adam Wharton is supposedly on their wishlist but with a £100m price tag, the expense could be a little too much. City have reportedly put in a call to Selhurst Park but received a swift rebuffing in response. Considering the proximity of that Sainsbury’s to the Palace ground, any potential purchase of a midfielder would come with a lot of Nectar points. With Savinho on his way to Tottenham, City could replace him with Allan Elias, a left-footed right winger at Palmeiras – a team not keen on selling. Ruben Amorim is eager on a return to Manchester but only to take Rúben Dias to Milan.

Over at Anfield there are plans afoot for Liverpool to bid £55m for Endrick to test Real Madrid’s mettle on the matter. The Brazilian spent time on loan at Lyon last season and was recently linked with Aston Villa, who could re-enter the race should Ollie Watkins head to Al-Hilal.

There is still a good chance of a Chelsea clearout, with Nicolas Jackson chatting with Napoli over a move to Italy, while Atlético Madrid are also keen. Palace are in the market for a centre-back and are keen on signing up Blues bomb squad member Axel Disasi. The Frenchman is unwanted at Stamford Bridge, so would be a relatively straightforward signing after previous loan spells with Aston Villa and West Ham. Auxerre’s Kevin Danois is another player Pierre Sage likes the look of, with the 22-year-old midfielder marketed at £25m.

On thing that could sour the mood at Selhurst Park is the departure of frontman Jean-Philippe Mateta who is getting admiring glances from Tottenham. The Frenchman has been tipped to move on for a while and is into the final year of his contract, which could force Palace to cash in.

The latest news from Hull’s transfer tombola has linked them to Oussama Targhalline of Feyenoord. A bid has already been faxed to the Netherlands but Porto, Atalanta and Bologna are also in in pursuit of the midfielder.

Leeds, Liverpool and Everton are in the hat for Midtjylland winger Darío Osorio. The Chilean shown great promise in Denmark and the Europa League, and could become one of the finds of the window if someone stumps the cash. If you like a bit of niche on your bingo card, then Polish side Radomiak Radom having a loan offer for Leeds youngster Alfie Cresswell rejected is right up there.

Burnley are nervous about losing Zian Flemming before the end of this window, with Lille ramping up their interest in the forward.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for as the new season kicks off
Sports.content:
1 Nwaneri out of Arsenal picture

While Myles Lewis-Skelly looks likely to remain at the Emirates, the same can’t be said for Ethan Nwaneri. The 19-year-old was outstanding in his breakthrough season for Arsenal in 2024-25 but barely featured last season and was sent on loan to Marseille. That didn’t really work out and Arsenal are now exploring another temporary move to ensure Nwaneri gets regular football this season. Milan, RB Leipzig, Dortmund and Fulham are all thought to be interested, with Nwaneri unlikely to feature on the bench for Friday’s opener against Coventry as a result. Whether Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus are available remains to be seen as Arsenal attempt to find suitors for the Brazil duo. Ed Aarons

Arsenal v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times BST)

2 New United pair down for Tigers test

Manchester United’s summer transfer business has focused on recruiting in central midfield. It will be interesting to see who Michael Carrick selects in two key roles for the first game of the season. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans have been present for more of pre-season than Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute for England at the World Cup and was a late returner to Carrington after a holiday. Carlos Baleba surely will not have arrived in time to start at Hull. Mainoo is in the best position in the long term but if Carrick decides to ease him into the season, it would be intriguing to see how Santos and Tielemans team up, the stress test for a new partnership that could provide the perfect balance of defensive awareness and ability to move the team up the pitch. Will Unwin

Hull City v Manchester United, Saturday 12.30pm

3 Swapped pair face former clubs

Neither Everton nor Crystal Palace have enjoyed a particularly scintillating summer of transfer activity but combined to make headlines with a swap deal between Dwight McNeil and Brennan Johnson. The pair will face one another – and their former clubs - on the first weekend of the season, eager to prove what their worth to their new teams. McNeil was rarely a regular on Merseyside but had a positive second half to last season, ironically after a move to Crystal Palace fell through at the last minute. Johnson did not settle at Selhurst Park, unable to crack the code that would get him into the starting lineup on a weekly basis, after moving from Spurs. A fresh start should reinvigorate the duo and there is no better way to further boost the mood than beating a former employer. WU

Everton v Crystal Palace, Saturday 3pm

4 Can Ipswich copy Black Cats’ success?

Ipswich clearly learned a lot from what Sunderland did a year ago, as they went out and bought a lot of players. The Black Cats quickly moulded their 19 acquisitions into a successful unit but at least they had the positive of a head coach in Régis Le Bris who had his feet under the table. Gary O’Neil is the new man at Portman Road and he has 12 signings – at time of writing – to potentially use for the opener. The record arrival, Emersonn, who has moved to Portman Road from Toulouse, is the most eye-catching of those who have been acquired. The Brazilian has an underwhelming career goalscoring record and a few question marks hanging over his head. Even though it is their first game, Ipswich need to pick up points at home, and to do so require a striker who can cause problems for defenders. How quickly Emersonn adapts will be critical for the Tractor Boys’ success this year. WU

Ipswich Town v Sunderland, Saturday 3pm

View image in fullscreen Emersonn is one of a number of big-money signings made by promoted Ipswich this summer. Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

5 Glasner’s tough Diomande ready for debut

August is the season for debuts and no one will be more satisfied than Oliver Glasner when Ousmane Diomande steps over the white line at the City Ground. Glasner wanted the Ivorian centre-back to replace Marc Guéhi at Crystal Palace, six months before the England defender departed for Manchester City. Diomande, a £34m buy from Sporting, is expected to line up in a back three for Nottingham Forest against Leeds, when the Austria midfielder Xaver Schlager, who played for Glasner at Wolfsburg, could also make his Forest bow. Diomande is a quick and physical defender but another aspect of his appeal is his aerial power at set pieces. “They’ve both played Champions League football and they are used to competing for titles,” said Glasner. “They can add this winning mentality.” Ben Fisher

Nottingham Forest v Leeds, Saturday 3pm

6 Serene Senesi can bring calm to Spurs

Cristian Romero has taken his maverick brand of defending to Atlético Madrid, upsetting neutral Premier League watchers. His compatriot Marcos Senesi has arrived to shore up things at the back as Roberto De Zerbi desperately tries to steer Spurs away from a third straight season of battling relegation. The all-action Romero had his qualities as a leader and defender but never felt dependable, which is what most want from a centre-back and captain. Senesi impressed during his time at Bournemouth, rarely making headlines but proving himself a calm presence at the back. The Argentinian is good on the ball and will be more adventurous in possession than his countryman. He is yet to be sent off in three seasons as a Premier League player – Romero was dismissed twice in 2025-26 alone, not to mention a one-match ban and a fine for his behaviour towards a referee. His calmness will improve Spurs. WU

Brentford v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm

7 Villa head south besieged by problems

It is surely not how Unai Emery envisaged the countdown to Aston Villa’s season-opener at Brighton on Sunday – and certainly not as he enjoyed the afterglow from the club’s Europa League triumph over Freiburg in May. The manager has an extraordinary number of problems. Take the midfield where the new signings João Gomes and Johan Manzambi are injury doubts. Note: Amadou Onana is a long-term casualty while Youri Tielemans has been sold. It goes on. Emery is about to lose Ezri Konsa to Arsenal – in a summer where Villa have also sold Morgan Rogers and Lucas Digne. They are trying to move on Emi Martínez, while the future of Ollie Watkins is uncertain, with Al-Hilal circling. For the cherry on top, the rampaging 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo is a fitness concern. Emery’s teamsheet will be very interesting. Will he pitch the new goalkeeper, Zion Suzuki, who only signed on Wednesday, straight in? David Hytner

Brighton v Aston Villa, Sunday 2pm

8 Maresca must win to silence City noise

Is Enzo Maresca already under pressure after Manchester City’s 3-0 schooling by Arsenal in the Community Shield? Maybe not, but if the Italian’s new team go down at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, you do not have to be a soothsayer to picture the scrutiny that will follow. Maresca and City are enduring a difficult transfer window, with Rodri’s departure to Barcelona the headline, a dizzying blow that has to be shaken off. The new Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, has faced City six times in the Champions League with Leipzig and Mönchengladbach, and is sure to order his visitors to go for the jugular at the Etihad. City are vulnerable but Maresca can remedy this with a win of any sort. This, after all, is the job many felt he was the obvious choice for. Jamie Jackson

Manchester City v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm

View image in fullscreen Anything but a win for Manchester City at home to Bournemouth will increase scrutiny on Enzo Maresca. Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPA

9 King Kev remembered at Newcastle

Kevin Keegan was supposed to have been the guest of honour at St James’ Park on Sunday, but his death from cancer in July means this meeting of two of his old clubs will turn into a tribute to one of English football’s enduring heroes. Keegan’s family will be present to witness an outpouring of love for the former Liverpool and Newcastle forward and (twice) Magpies manager. Once the game kicks off, all eyes will be on Alexander Isak, a St James’ Park old boy whose decision to force a £125m move to Anfield last summer did not go down well on Tyneside. The Sweden striker, making his first return to Newcastle, has much to prove at Liverpool, and now has a new head coach to impress in Andoni Iraola. Newcastle too have a new face in the home dugout, where Matthias Jaissle will occupy the technical area for so long inhabited by Eddie Howe. Louise Taylor

Newcastle v Liverpool, Sunday 4.30pm

10 Former Madrid managers meet in capital

Real Madrid’s two head coaches from last season meet at Craven Cottage, with the focus on Xabi Alonso, rather than Álvaro Arbeloa. The Fulham man, however, may have more to prove in the Premier League. His managerial career has been less prominent than that of his Basque rival – and he has clearly insisted on snapping up talent from the Bernabéu. Gonzalo García and César Palacios have made the trip over from the Spanish capital with Arbeloa. It shows great faith from the former Liverpool defender but it does put extra pressure on the trio, their fates now permanently intertwined. All three need a positive start to show they merit being in the Premier League. Otherwise, it would be very easily to criticise them individually and collectively. WU

Sports.title: European playoffs: Rangers scrape first-leg win as Brighton draw in Norway
Sports.content:
Ryan Naderi’s second-half strike gave an unconvincing Rangers a narrow 1-0 win in the first leg of their Conference League playoff tie against Czech side Jablonec at Ibrox. Derek McInnes got his first win as Rangers manager at the fifth time of asking with a 5-1 thumping of St Mirren on Sunday but there was regression in the goalless first half which brought boos at the interval whistle.

The Govan side pepped up after the break and Naderi opened the scoring from close range in the 50th minute but in the 78th minute the substitute Cammy Devlin was sent off – minutes after coming off the bench – for a high tackle on Jiri Slama to leave Rangers to see out the game with 10 men.

Fabian Hürzeler, admitted: “It’s not the result we hoped for,” after Brighton were held to a frustrating goalless draw against Tromsø in Norway. The Seagulls, who open the new domestic campaign against Aston Villa on Sunday, created several good chances but could not find a way past the Tromsø keeper Jakob Haugaard.

View image in fullscreen Brighton players applaud the fans after their draw at Tromsø. Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images

The winger Ibrahim Osman – making his Brighton debut after three loan spells away – looked particularly lively during the first half. Tromsø then almost snatched a late winner on the break, but the defender Isak Vadebu sent his shot wide as the tie went into next week’s second leg at the Amex Stadium all square.

Hearts’ head coach, Wouter Vrancken, hopes James Wilson’s stunning goal in the 2-2 Conference League draw with Rapid Vienna is a sign of things to come from the youngster. He drilled in an unstoppable drive from 30 yards just moments after coming on as the hosts took the lead in the playoff first leg.

“He’s a young lad so for sure it will be extra special. Let’s hope he can make the next steps,” Vrancken said.

Wilson’s effort marked an impressive turnaround after Josh McPade cancelled out Serge-Philippe Raux-Yao’s first-half header. However, Rapid scrambled in a late equaliser through Nikolaus Wumbrand to ensure the tie remains on a knife edge ahead of next week’s return leg.

David Gray, the Hibernian head coach, savoured “a massive performance and a massive result” as his side kept themselves on course to reach the main phase with a spirited 0-0 draw in Belgium against Gent.

For the second Thursday night in a row, Hibs ground out a stalemate on foreign soil after they eliminated Shkendija in North Macedonia last week. It could have been even better for them if Owen Elding’s 15th-minute penalty had not been saved by Davy Roef.

Motherwell made a whirlwind start at home to Freiburg, with Regan Charles-Cook sidefooting in Emmanuel Longelo’s cutback after just 73 seconds. But Matthias Ginter headed Freiburg level on 27 minutes and netted a second from the spot, after Martin Moormann was shown a straight red card on 65 minutes via a video assistant referee review.

The substitute Keisuke Goto added a third with a stoppage-time header to leave the Scottish side with a 3-1 deficit mountain to climb in Germany next Thursday.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Northern Irish champions, Larne, took a big step towards the league phase after a 2-0 win at 10-man Lincoln Red Imps.

The match looked set to finish goalless in Gibraltar after Red Imps had held firm following Yussef Flalhi’s 29th-minute red card. However, visiting Larne made their pressure pay when Paul O’Neill struck with five minutes left before fellow substitute Kevin O’Hara’s stoppage-time breakaway goal ensured Gary Haveron’s side will have a cushion ahead of the second leg at Inver Park.

Shamrock were held to a 1-1 draw at home by the Finnish side KuPS after they conceded an 85th-minute equaliser. The former Sheffield United full-back Enda Stevens put the Irish side ahead after 49 minutes, but they were denied a precious victory when the one-time Charlton youngster Piotr Parzyszek levelled late on at Tallaght Stadium.

View image in fullscreen Mohamed Salah had a tricky night against Ferencvaros. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

In the Europa League, Mohamed Salah played all 90 minutes of his home debut as Trabzonspor hosted Ferencvaros, but the Hungarian side won 1-0 and their Turkish opponents had Chibuike Nwaiwu sent off in added time.

Sports.title: Maracanã to host opening game and final at next year’s Women’s World Cup
Sports.content:
The Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro will host the opening game and the final of next year’s Women’s World Cup. The 78,838-capacity stadium, which hosted the finals of the 1950 and 2014 men’s World Cups as well as the finals of the Olympic football competitions in 2016, will be the venue for Brazil’s opening Group A match on 24 June, before staging the final on 25 July.

Fifa released the schedule for all 64 matches for the tournament, which features 32 teams. The draw will take place after more of the qualification playoffs have been contested.

Brazil will also play group matches at the Arena Itaquera in São Paulo – which will host 10 matches at the finals, more than any other host city – and at the Estádio Nacional in Brasília. Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo have been selected to host the semi‑finals, with the latter also staging the third-fourth playoff. All eight of the stadiums involved in the finals staged matches at the men’s tournament in 2014.

Belo Horizonte – the scene of Brazil’s humiliating 7-1 semi-final loss to Germany 12 years ago – has been chosen to host a quarter-final. The winners of Group A will play in that quarter-final if they progress that far. Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo will host the three other quarter-finals.

Porto Alegre and Recife are also staging matches in the 10th official edition of the Women’s World Cup and the second to include 32 teams, after the expanded tournament, cohosted by Australia and New Zealand, in 2023.

Spain won the title for the first time in Sydney after victory over England.

View image in fullscreen Spain beat England in the final of the 2023 Women’s World Cup to lift the trophy for the first time. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/Getty Images

“We can’t wait to witness a new chapter of women’s football history unfold when the world’s best players, coaches, fans and local communities take centre stage in Brazil next year,” said Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino. “I already have goosebumps thinking about the incredible passion, colour and energy that Brazilian fans will bring to the tournament.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The former Brazil captain Aline Pellegrino said: “Each host city will add its ​own unique flavour, making ​this a colourful, joyful ​and unforgettable celebration. The ​world’s best players ‌will feel that ​energy from ​the stands and they will give it back on the pitch through moments and performances that will inspire girls and boys around the world.”

It is the first time the women’s event has been staged in South America and the Maracanã will join the now-demolished Råsunda Stadium in Solna, Sweden, and the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California, as having hosted World Cup finals for both the men’s and women’s game.

Sports.title: Countdown rule introduced to Premier League and could see opposing team awarded a corner
Sports.content:
Countdown rule introduced to Premier League and could see opposing team awarded a corner

As top-flight action returns, the PGMOL has confirmed a brand-new 'five-second' restart rule that could directly hand opposition teams goal-scoring opportunities.

Ahead of the new Premier League season, the Football Association confirmed several key updates to the 'Laws of the Game'.

3 The new anti-time-wasting rules significantly reduced delays at the World Cup Credit: Getty

Referees have made it their goal to speed up effective playing time, targeting deliberate delays over goal-kicks and throw-ins.

One of the most dramatic additions is a strict five-second countdown for set-piece restarts, featuring an immediate possession reversal if the time limit is exceeded.

Handing away throw-ins or conceding cheap corners could prove disastrous for teams trying to close out tight matches.

What is the Premier League's five-second restart rule?

Under the new law, match officials will actively initiate a five-second countdown whenever a player is deemed to be unnecessarily delaying the taking of a throw-in or goal-kick.

Referees will begin counting after using an arm motion to signal the countdown if players take too long to retrieve the ball or deliberately waste time positioning it.

If play is not restarted before the countdown finishes, the referee will enforce an immediate penalty.

For throw-ins, possession is forfeited, and a throw-in is awarded to the opposing team at the exact same spot.

For goal-kicks, a corner kick is awarded to the opposing side.

3 319 set-piece goals were scored in the Premier League last season Credit: Getty

Premier League 26/27 opening fixtures 3pm kick-offs unless stated Friday, August 22 Arsenal vs Coventry - 8pm, live on talkSPORT Saturday, August 23 Hull vs Manchester United - 12.30pm, live on talkSPORT

Everton vs Crystal Palace

Ipswich vs Sunderland

Nottingham Forest vs Leeds

Brentford vs Tottenham - 5.30pm Sunday, August 24 Brighton vs Aston Villa - 2pm

Manchester City vs Bournemouth - 2pm

Newcastle vs Liverpool - 4.30pm Monday, August 25 Fulham vs Chelsea - 8pm, live on talkSPORT

Why is the Premier League enforcing it?

Goalkeepers and defenders have often used routine restarts late in matches to disrupt the flow of play.

They often slowly walk to the ball or place it down multiple times to kill time.

Prior to the rule change, officials could only punish these tactics by issuing a yellow card.

It was a sanction players would willingly accept during injury time.

By threatening players with a counter-attacking opportunity, the PGMOL expects players to restart play far more quickly.

With set-piece goals proving crucial in the Premier League last season, taking five seconds too long over a goal-kick could prove the difference in securing three points this campaign.

The system was well integrated into the World Cup this summer, with players maintaining the usual flow of the game - even in high-stake moments.

However, some players appeared to have come up with a way around the new rule change, including Scotland's Andy Robertson.

3 Fans spotted Robertson's throw-in hack during Scotland's group stage win over Haiti Credit: Getty

The Tartan Army captain was spotted signalling his teammates into position before picking up the ball.

As a result, the referee did not start the countdown for him to take the throw-in, allowing his side extra time to reset while holding a 1-0 lead to Haiti.

The rule will also be enforced throughout English football in both the men's and women's game, including in the EFL, the WSL, and the National League.

Sports.title: New Premier League substitution rule could see players banned for entering pitch
Sports.content:
New Premier League substitution rule could see players banned for entering pitch

The Premier League is back and managers and players will need to navigate a host of major rule changes designed to stamp out time-wasting.

The PGMOL has confirmed a brand-new substitution law that could leave teams a player down.



3 No player received the sanction at the 2026 World Cup Credit: Getty

Refereeing chiefs have made it their mission to speed up the game following the implementation of new regulations at the World Cup.

They want to target the tactical thinking of footballers taking slow, deliberate walks across the pitch when their number is raised on the board.

The new rule will only allow a strict 10-second time limit for substituted players to leave the pitch.



Failure to do so will force clubs to play with only ten men, and could prove disastrous for teams protecting a tight lead late on.

What is the Premier League's 10-second substitution rule?

Under the new law, a player being substituted has exactly ten seconds to completely leave the pitch once the electronic board is displayed by the fourth official.



Additionally, players must exit using the nearest point on the boundary line, unless directed otherwise by the match officials for safety or security reasons.

If a player takes longer than the allocated time to cross the touchline, their replacement is barred from entering the field for at least one minute.



Their team must play temporarily with a reduced side until the first natural stoppage after that minute has elapsed.

3 Michael Oliver will be used to the rule after refereeing at the summer tournament Credit: Getty

Why is the Premier League enforcing it?

For years, Premier League managers have used late substitutions to disrupt momentum and run down the clock.

Previously, referees could only punish slow exits by showing a yellow card to the departing player.



The old sanction rarely discouraged teams from employing the tactic late in matches.

By forcing a club to play with a man down for over a minute, the PGMOL expects players to sprint off the pitch to avoid leaving their teammates vulnerable.

Following the successful introduction of the measures at the World Cup during the summer, the FA was keen to adopt the set of rules for English football.

The rule will also be implemented across the men's and women's professional game in England, including the EFL, WSL Football and the National League



3 Goalkeepers are often accused of faking injury to waste time, but this trial is designed to stop that Credit: Getty

What other rules have been introduced?

Goalkeepers will also be subjected to new regulations.

If play stops for a keeper injury, they must also leave the pitch upon restart like any other player - unless the stoppage involves a direct collision or is a serious issue.

Pro Ref released a statement saying: "The trial, championed collectively by Pro Ref, The FA, Premier League, EFL, WSL Football and the National League, will be implemented across the men's and women's professional game in England,

"And is designed to address occasions where goalkeeper injuries have been used to disrupt momentum, slow the game down or create opportunities for tactical instruction."



Meanwhile, any outfield player who receives on-pitch treatment must now remain off the field for a minimum of 60 seconds - doubled from the previous 30 seconds.

Additionally, referees will enforce a five-second countdown for throw-ins and goal-kicks, with a potential reversal of possession for delays.

VAR can now review second yellow card incidents, though a high threshold for intervention remains in place for other decisions.

There will also be increased focus on penalising holding in the box that materially impacts play.

Sports.title: Is the hand over mouth red card rule being used in Premier League this season?
Sports.content:
Is the hand over mouth red card rule being used in Premier League this season?

The World Cup debuted several new rules this summer, not least the introduction of red cards for players covering their mouths.

Paraguay's Miguel Almiron became the first player to be sent off under the new law, before Arsenal defender Piero Hincapie saw red for the same reason in Ecuador's last-16 exit.

4 Piero Hincapie became the second victim to the World Cup's hand covering red card Credit: Getty

The strong measure was part of 11 rule changes brought in by FIFA specifically for the tournament.

It followed Vinicius Junior's report of alleged racist abuse from Gianluca Prestianni while covering his mouth with his shirt during Benfica vs Real Madrid in February.

Referees were quick to implement the new rule this summer, as shown with Almiron and Hincapie, and players soon cottoned on too.

Argentina icon Lionel Messi came under criticism after he tried to get Spain's Marc Cucurella sent off for covering his mouth during the World Cup final.

So, with a number of Premier League stars already familiar with the rule, will we continue to see it when club football returns this weekend?

Is the rule being used in the Premier League?

The short answer to this question is no, Premier League players won't be shown red cards for covering their mouths during confrontations.

Ahead of the 2026/27 season, English football's top-flight recently unveiled their new set of football principles and refereeing points.

Various measures were announced, including the clarification that yellow cards will now be awarded for hair pulling, having previously been deemed violent conduct and being punished with red cards.

But the Premier League won't be following FIFA's lead and introducing automatic reds to players who cover their mouths.

There is no mention of this in their new football principles, and it has already been confirmed that the rule won't feature in UEFA competitions.

4 Miguel Almiron paid the price after covering his mouth in a confrontation with a Turkey player during the World Cup's group stage Credit: Getty

Midway through the World Cup, European football's governing body confirmed it would not be taking up the option to use the law in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League.

That is despite the rule featuring at the World Cup following the Prestianni incident, which happened in UEFA's premier competition.

The Benfica winger was ultimately handed a six-game ban by UEFA for homophobic conduct, having been accused of racially abusing Vinicius Junior whilst covering his mouth with his shirt.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino enforced the rule in the World Cup just two weeks after the incident.

What new rules are being introduced in the Premier League?

While we won't be seeing an red cards handed out for mouth covering just yet, fans will need to be aware of other rule changes in the upcoming Premier League season.

As well as yellow cards for hair pulls, the World Cup's crackdown on time wasting will continue in English football.

4 Michael Oliver will be among the Premier League referees tasked with implementing their new rules Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Premier League 26/27 opening fixtures 3pm kick-offs unless stated Friday, August 22 Arsenal vs Coventry - 8pm, live on talkSPORT Saturday, August 23 Hull vs Manchester United - 12.30pm, live on talkSPORT

Manchester City vs Bournemouth - 2pm

Newcastle vs Liverpool - 4.30pm Monday, August 25 Fulham vs Chelsea - 8pm, live on talkSPORT

The goalkeeper eight-second rule will continue to feature in the Premier League following its implementation last season.

Additionally, referees will enforce a five-second countdown for throw-ins and goal-kicks, with delayed restarts potentially resulting in possession being overturned.

This system was used at the World Cup, while another VAR measure introduced in the summer will also be rolled out in English football.

VAR will again be able to review incidents where a player is shown a second yellow card that results in a red card.

Meanwhile, any outfield player who receives on-pitch treatment must now remain off the field for a minimum of 60 seconds - doubled from the previous 30 seconds.

There will also be a 10-second limit for players leaving the pitch when substituted.

4 There should be fewer instances of goalkeepers receiving treatment from physios after another new rule is trialled Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

If they exceed the limit, the replacement player must wait until the next stoppage after one minute has passed before entering.

Meanwhile, a radical new rule is set to be trialled to tackle goalkeeper tactical timeouts.

If play stops for an injury to a shot stopper, they must also leave the pitch upon restart like any other player - unless the stoppage involves a direct collision or is a serious issue.

Now, if the game is stopped for this reason, the manager will have to nominate an outfield player to leave the pitch immediately, who will stay off the pitch for at least one minute after the restart of play.

Sports.title: When is the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony? Harry Kane in the running for prestigious award
Sports.content:
When is the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony? Harry Kane in the running for prestigious award

The winner of the 2026 Ballon d'Or will soon be announced at a star-studded ceremony.

London will host the 70th edition of the award ceremony in October.

4 The 2026 Ballon d'Or winner will be revealed at a star-studded ceremony in London Credit: Getty

This year's award will be handed out based on performances during the 2025/26 season as well as this summer's World Cup.

France Football's cut-off dates for the latest Ballon d'Or stretched from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026.

Ousmane Dembele is the current holder of the prestigious award after winning for the first time last year.

The Paris Saint-Germain forward was honoured ahead of Lamine Yamal and Vitinha following his side's treble triumph.

When is the 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony?

The 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony will be held on Monday, October 2026.

Although an exact venue has yet to be announced, the gala will be held in London.

A total of 30 players will be nominated for the award, with last year's nominees named in August.

However, the previous ceremony was held earlier than this year's on September 22, 2025.

The nominees were named 46 days before the ceremony, which would see this year's revealed on Thursday, September 10.

4 Kane is seen by many as the leading candidate to win the 2026 Ballon d'Or Credit: Getty

Who is the favourite for the 2026 Ballon d'Or?

Harry Kane is among the leading candidates for this year's Ballon d'Or.

The England captain is seen by many as the front runner for the award.

However, Yamal is expected to rival Kane after winning the World Cup with Spain to add to Barcelona's LaLiga title victory.

World Cup golden boot winner Kylian Mbappe is also in the mix following his 10-goal haul at the tournament for France.

Kane himself found the net six times as the Three Lions finished third in North America, their best performance since 1966.

Those goals took his overall tally for club and country in the 2025/26 season to 73 across all competitions.

Kane's form in front of goal last term has already secured him a second Gerd Muller Trophy, awarded to the highest-scoring player of the season.

4 Kane scored 73 goals for club and country during the 2025/26 season Credit: AFP

Last 10 Ballon d'Or winners 2015: Lionel Messi 2016: Cristiano Ronaldo 2017: Cristiano Ronaldo 2018: Luka Modric 2019: Lionel Messi 2021: Lionel Messi 2022: Karim Benzema 2023: Lionel Messi 2024: Rodri 2025: Ousmane Dembele

He previously shared the award with Mbappe in 2024 after they both scored 52 goals for club and country.

As well as scoring 12 times for England, he was on target 61 times in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich.

Those goals included 36 in the Bundesliga as he won a second European Golden Shoe.

Kane also helped his side lift by the league title and the DFB Pokal in an historic double.

His previous best finish in the Ballon d'Or is 10th, which he achieved in 2017, 2018 and 2024.

The 33-year-old is aiming to become the fifth Englishman to win the award and the first since Michael Owen in 2001.

4 World Cup winner Yamal is also in the running for the prestigious award Credit: Getty

2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony awards Ballon d'Or

Ballon d'Or Feminin

Men's Kopa Trophy - Best Under-21 player

Women's Kopa Trophy

Men's Yashin Trophy - Best goalkeeper

Women's Yashin Trophy

Gerd Muller Trophy - Highest-scoring footballer

Socrates Award - Recognises humanitarian work

Men's Club of the Year

Women's Club of the Year

Men's Coach of the Year

Women's Coach of the Year

How is the Ballon d'Or winner chosen?

France Football's criteria for the Ballon d'Or voting process outlines three requirements for the award winner.

The trophy is to be awarded to a player based on their individual performances as well as decisive and impressive character.

Team performances and achievements such as trophies must also be considered.

Meanwhile, class and fair play are also to be taken into consideration by voters.

The winner is voted for by an international jury of football journalists.

They consist of one representative from each country in the top 100 of FIFA's World Rankings.

Sports.title: Why bother trying to compete if you’re not the ‘Big Six’? The Premier League is a closed shop
Sports.content:
Why bother trying to compete if you’re not the ‘Big Six’? The Premier League is a closed shop

Everton have not won silverware since 1995, yet under modern financial regulations they are being told to shut up and accept mid-table mediocrity.

If a club outside the established elite dares to dream into breaking English football's top tier, the current system is engineered to slam the door straight in their face.

6 The last time Everton competed in European football was in 2017/18 Credit: Getty

The Toffees were docked eight points in the 2023/24 season after breaching the Profit and Sustainability Rules - a penalty driven largely by the soaring costs of financing their new stadium.

The threat of relegation could have proved fatal to the historic club's ongoing existence.

Meanwhile, Chelsea made more than £47million in secret payments to help build a team that achieved immense success - titles, domestic glory and two Champions League triumphs. Their punishment? A £10.75m fine and a transfer ban that is unlikely to come into effect.

Additionally, Manchester City are still waiting to hear the final verdict of their 115 financial charges - and it has now been 21 months since a three-person commission concluded its initial hearing.

Everton were dangerously close to the drop for two consecutive campaigns following their point deductions, but they have since found stability under the returning David Moyes, finishing safely in 13th for the last two seasons.

It should not be forgotten that the Merseyside-based team were a part of the original 'Big Five' - alongside Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal, and Tottenham - that helped form the Premier League in 1992.

However, they inevitably fell behind after they missed the early commercial boom and were overtaken by the billionaire owners of Chelsea and Man City.

Reflecting on the glass ceiling facing historic clubs like Everton, talkSPORT's Gabby Agbonlahor explained how they could never disrupt the status quo with the current setup.

He said: "I think Everton will always be stuck in mid-table, it’s really hard now to try and challenge the top six because if you do… the rules go against you, and I’m sick of talking about it."

The harsh reality facing modern football is that under current financial regulations, ambition becomes an unsustainable habit. Once a club tastes success, they are financially penalised for attempting to maintain the spending required to remain at the top table.

6 Everton managed to stay up twice consecutively on the final game of the season following their points deductions Credit: Getty

Perhaps, under these rules, remaining in mid-table is the safest option?

Villa and Newcastle forced to sell

Look no further than Aston Villa and Newcastle. Both clubs have made heroic pushes into the Champions League in recent campaigns and ended long silverware droughts.

Eddie Howe guided Newcastle to the Carabao Cup and Unai Emery led Villa to Europa League glory.

However, both sides have found themselves constrained by spending rules, forced to sell key players to 'Big Six' rivals simply to balance the books and avoid severe points deductions.

Villa perspective talkSPORT writer and Aston Villa fan Alex Conrad says: Imagine winning a European trophy, qualifying for the Champions League, and finishing fourth in the Premier League. Pretty good, right? Now imagine the core of the squad that helped achieve all of those things has been ripped out, simply to help balance the financial books. That is, tragically, the price of success for Aston Villa. Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Morgan Rogers have all departed, with Ezri Konsa set to follow them out the door. The high-profile exits may not be done just yet, with Ollie Watkins and Emi Martinez both facing uncertain futures. If losing up to six of your starting line-up is the reward for the best season in recent history, what is the point of reaching for the stars? How can clubs genuinely aspire to win the Premier League, like Richard Masters says, when the 'Big Six' can weaken their domestic rivals when they feel like it? Yes, there is the argument that those same teams have built strong revenue streams, and I have no issues with that. But Villa, Newcastle or any other club who boast sufficient financial and competitive strength to upset the apple cart do not deserve to have their ambitions quashed by a set of outdated financial rules. By not altering them, it only fuels the argument that the Premier League has well and truly become a closed shop.

Despite these concerns, the CEO of the Premier League Richard Masters, maintained that financial restrictions do not prevent ambitious clubs from mounting title challenges.

Speaking to talkSPORT, he said: "Either you take the view that there should be no financial rules, or you should be able to spend as long as you can show you can afford it - I think our league would look very different.

6 Masters is hopeful the new squad cost ratio rules will improve the Premier League Credit: Getty

"Premier League clubs don’t want that, they do want financial regulation but they may all have a different version of the financial rules they would want for themselves.

"Villa have been in Europe four times in a row, twice in the Champions League, they won their first trophy for a very long time, I know they would like to kick on from here but they’ve had fantastic success.

"Newcastle have had a season of change, players are leaving but they signed new ones, new manager, who knows what’s going to happen. That’s the excitement of the Premier League, everyone should be able to aspire and that's been proven in the last four to five seasons."

However, ex-Crystal Palace owner Simon Jordan questioned that defence, exposing the system as a way to force ambitious sides to dismantle their squads the moment they 'overachieve'.

6 The Newcastle team that won the Carabao Cup has completely changed now Credit: Getty

He said: "Masters doesn’t get challenged properly, tell me how you can expect non big six clubs to compete. Aston Villa have been sanctioned by UEFA and they’ve had to sell their best players to balance their books. Top clubs do not have to do that."

He added: "Aston Villa have got an excellent manager that will eventually be poached by a bigger club than them. They'll go back round in a circle.

"They'll sell their best players like Newcastle have been forced to do. Like Aston Villa have often been forced to manage their books. To manage their circumstances.

Newcastle perspective talkSPORT writer and Newcastle fan Jack Cunningham said: PSR or SCR (or whatever stupid acronym they use these days), the true killer of dreams unless you are part of the 'big six'. I am going to take you back to March 2025 and Newcastle United have just ended 70 years of domestic pain by winning the Carabao Cup. It is a moment that generations of Toon fans will hold onto forever, and increasingly, it is looking as if that is as good as it will get. And if that is the case, then I wouldn't change it for anything, but when your club's owners are worth around £320billion that first trophy should be the start of something great, a new force in the Premier League. Instead, Newcastle have sold Alexander Isak, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali all to direct Premier League rivals, strengthening them and weakening us, forcing the club to plump for as yet, unproven talent. Now, last summer's transfer window was a failure, with a lot of the players signed struggling in black and white, but because of some arbitrary rules about revenue dressed up to 'protect clubs', Newcastle have been forced to sell while we've seen Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur and Manchester United waste money, not have to sell their best players and go again. It means there are no real consequences for those clubs, while Newcastle have been essentially punished for daring to challenge the establishment, and a season of transition awaits, while those they want to catch get stronger. I am not advocating for a free-for-all as Newcastle would then blow everyone out of the water, but a relaxation in the rules to allow us to compete and create a better product with eight or nine clubs fighting for the Champions League spots and title every year would elevate the Premier League to another level.

"Liverpool, Arsenal, Manchester United - they don't have to manage their books do they? They go out and spend like drunken sailors because they've got the turnover.

"How do Newcastle or Aston Villa get a £600million turnover? They might be able to do it in ten years time when the turnover of Liverpool, Man United, Man City becomes £900million."

Everton can demand what they want

Unlike the two sides who are caught in a desperate juggling act to maintain European football, Everton have instead been stuck in neutral.

6 Aston Villa won their first trophy since 1996, and have somehow lost four of their key players from the starting 11 in the Europa League final, with another two players looking likely to leave Credit: TNT Sports

While Villa secured Champions League qualification and lifted the Europa League, they fell into a severe financial bottleneck. After breaching spending thresholds, Villa were placed under a strict 'one-in, one-out' transfer policy via a UEFA Settlement Agreement.

Emery's side are subject to harsher restrictions of keeping their squad cost below 70 per cent of their revenue due to qualifying for European football, while Everton missed out - meaning they only have to comply with the Premier League regulatory body.

Ironically, the Toffees have the ability to negotiate transfers on their own terms simply because mediocrity has protected them from the harsher European spending traps catching out top-six challengers.

You don't see Moyes selling Everton's key assets of Iliman Ndiaye or James Garner because he is not forced to sell them and able to value his players at whatever price he wants.

The Leicester warning

Look at Leicester City. The Foxes pulled off the greatest miracle in modern sporting history by winning the Premier League in 2016, yet the system eventually caught up with them.

6 Leicester have started the new season in the third tier Credit: Getty

The financial strain of trying to organically bridge the gap to the elite ultimately triggered their painful downfall to League One. If Villa or Newcastle were to break the rules, things could become nasty similarly to the previous champions of England.

While the current financial framework appears setup for non 'big six' clubs to fail, teams must also exercise internal responsibility to ensure sustainable operation.

Leicester perspective talkSPORT writer and Leicester fan Jack Johnson said: Leicester City were Premier League champions a decade ago and at the top of the world, toppling the Big Six and making history. But 10 years later, they're all the way down in League One. Now, some may think that came from the strict Premier League rules and 'making sure the Big Six aren't beaten again'. But in Leicester's case, it's almost all self-inflicted. Their mismanagement of finances from the top of the club has doomed them, with monstrous losses being recorded every single year from 2021 onward. PSR rules did lead to multiple charges for the Foxes, which eventually led to a points deduction last season, however, there was not much to complain about when looking at their horror figures.

While financial regulations currently seem structured to protect the traditional elite, regulators must be careful not to simply expand the hierarchy into an artificial 'Big Eight'.

Equally, ambitious clubs and owners should not be punished for wanting to invest and compete at the highest level.

So... with a tongue in cheek, maybe it's best for Everton that they don't win anything anytime soon.

Sports.title: ‘Don’t see it’ – Man United warned marquee signing is not good enough to play for them
Sports.content:
‘Don’t see it’ – Man United warned marquee signing is not good enough to play for them

talkSPORT host Jason Cundy believes Youri Tielemans is not good enough to play for Manchester United.

Tielemans secured a shock switch to Old Trafford last month after the Manchester giants triggered his £35million release clause.



2 Tielemans completed his £35million move to Manchester United last month Credit: Getty

The Belgian has been one of the Premier League's most consistent performers in recent seasons, and his departure is a blow for Aston Villa.

United fans, on the whole, are encouraged that Tielemans has completed his move to Michael Carrick's side.

However, ex-Chelsea defender Cundy has questioned United's decision to sign the Belgium international.



'I don't get it'

"I've never thought of Tielemans as a Man United player," Cundy said on The Sports Bar on Thursday night.

Former Tottenham midfielder Jamie O'Hara replied: "I think he's a good player. I think he's top. I think he's good enough to play for Man United.



"He ain't Paul Scholes, of course not. He was a very good player for Aston Villa last season. They've got Champions League football. They won the Europa League.

"And then he goes and signs for Man United."

Cundy shot back: "I don't get it. He's a good player, that's it.

"I don't see it. I don't see this big shift in Manchester United's midfield. I honestly don't."



2 Cundy doesn't get why Manchester United have signed Youri Tielemans Credit: Getty

O'Hara then replied: "You're saying he's not good enough to play for Man United."

"Maybe this year he is," Cundy added. "That's the point. Maybe he is now.

"But he should not be Man United's midfield. He should not be."

After some back and forth between the pair, Cundy continued: "To go to Man United. Maybe I'm missing it. Maybe I'm wrong. I can't see it."



O'Hara added: "I think he'll prove you wrong."

United's start to the season

United kick off their 2026/27 Premier League season with a trip to promoted Hull City in Saturday's lunchtime kick off, live on talkSPORT.

Tielemans is expected to start alongside fellow new signing Andrey Santos in the middle of the park when United face the Tigers.

Carrick's side then welcome Ipswich Town to Old Trafford for their first home game of the campaign next weekend.

United then take on Everton, Manchester City and Fulham before the first international break of the season.

Sports.title: UEFA in talks with two federations over Gianni Infantino vote of no confidence
Sports.content:
UEFA in talks with two federations over Gianni Infantino vote of no confidence

UEFA, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) are in talks over whether to table a vote of no confidence against FIFA President Gianni Infantino, talkSPORT understands.

Conversations were also had on the matter last week in Salzburg at the UEFA Super Cup, as revealed by talkSPORT.

3 Infantino's days as FIFA President appear to be numbered Credit: Getty

Senior figures within each confederation, including UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani, are lobbying federations to support an emergency vote.

Under FIFA’s statutes, an extraordinary congress can be convened if 43 of FIFA’s 211 member associations submit a written request.

UEFA alone, with 55 votes, has the power to trigger a vote of no confidence, but it is viewed as counter-intuitive unless the majority of FIFA members back it.

UEFA (55), Concacaf (35) and the AFC (46) hold 136 of the 211 votes but there is no guarantee all members side against Infantino.

The English, Irish, Northern Irish, Scottish and Welsh Football Associations have all already pulled support for Infantino.

Yet Mexico have broken Concacaf ranks in backing the FIFA President. And Infantino is hoping to gain more Concacaf support by attending the ongoing Under-14 Boys Challenge, an event staged by the Caribbean Football Union in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic.

Yet it is really Asia that is widely viewed as the key battleground for both Infantino and any challenger, or in the absence of one the success chance of a vote of no confidence passing.

The AFC wrote a joint letter calling for change along with UEFA and Concacaf. And the standout paragraph within it attacked Infantino in all but name.

"Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding - or demanding - power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it," the letter read.

"When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

3 The AFC President has been discussed as an option to be Infantino's successor Credit: Getty

However, Qatar have since thrown their support behind Infantino. Qatar Football Association President Sheikh Hamid bin Khalifa Al-Thani even wrote his own letter to the AFC Executive Committee, seen by talkSPORT, claiming the AFC bypassed any consultation process.

"What consultation, if any, was undertaken with AFC's Member Associations before the Statement was issued in their collective name?" Al-Thani asks.

"The AFC Reply does not identify a single Member Association that was consulted, does not describe any meeting, circular, or communication through which such consultation might have occurred, and does not point to any decision of the AFC Executive Committee authorising the Statement."

The QFA believe the AFC have broken governance protocol arguing the confederation's statutes don't allow a blanket position to be taken without speaking to all members.

Infantino also has support in Asia from Bhutan, the Philippines, and the UAE.

And now a key vote will be Saudi Arabia, who have remained silent so far during the crisis sparked by Infantino’s failed plans to privatise FIFA.

3 Saudi Arabia controversially won the World Cup rights two years ago Credit: Getty

This is due to Saudi Football Federation (SAFF) President Yasser Al Misehal standing down following Saudi Arabia's World Cup exit, and his replacement not being voted on until August 30.

Multiple Saudi executives, spoken to by talkSPORT, want the federation to remove their support for the FIFA President but it is unclear at this stage which side the country will take.

talkSPORT has learned Infantino hopes to travel to Saudi to meet the new SAFF President in a bid to lobby support. FIFA has been approached for comment.

If Saudi remove their support for Infantino it could create a domino effect with other federations in Asia following suit.

This will encourage AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who several FIFA insiders believe has aspirations to be FIFA President, but has no aspirations to go head-to-head against Infantino as it stands.

There appears to be consensus from many of Infantino's critics that it would be better he quits, but given the FIFA President has - to date - vowed to fight on, according to those familiar with his thinking.

A vote of no confidence remains possible between now and November 18.

November 18 is significant because it is the date by which prospective FIFA presidential candidates must commit to standing.

Once that deadline passes, it is viewed as redundant holding a vote of no confidence, since the election itself in March next year would then ultimately serve the same purpose.

Sports.title: New Premier League 2026-27 rules revealed: MORE VAR involvement, strictly timed substitutions - and the plan to crack down on time-wasting goalkeepers
Sports.content:
New Premier League 2026-27 rules revealed: MORE VAR involvement, strictly timed substitutions - and the plan to crack down on time-wasting goalkeepers

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Football officiating seems to be the hardest job in the game these days. It was, and is, never easy, as you will invariably upset at least one set of fans and players while holding the whistle.

Yet, in recent years, with uncertainty amongst supporters and clubs over the intricacies of the rules – and of course the introduction of VAR – it seems as if the job has become impossible.

Now, in the wake of the 2026 World Cup, the Professional Referee Group (Pro Ref – formerly PGMOL) has drawn up almost an entirely new set of rules to be implemented for the upcoming season for officials and fans to contend with.

Here, Daily Mail Sport examines the major changes ahead of the 2026-27 season coming into play from the start of Arsenal's curtain-raiser against Coventry...

New rules for the 2026-27 Premier League campaign

Goal-kick and throw-in countdowns

Since the beginning of last season's campaign, Premier League teams have seen a countdown implemented for goal-kicks to prevent timewasting and intentional provocation of the opponent. From this season onwards, this countdown rule will apply to throw-ins as well.

The refereeing body has made it clear that every goal-kick and throw-in will have exactly five seconds to be taken or the opposing team will receive a corner, or the throw-in will be turned over. This change ostensibly seems positive but may simply result in more controversy if not applied properly and consistently.

The Professional Referee Group (Pro Ref) have introduced a raft of new rules for 2026-27

More VAR involvement

The prospect of a lower threshold for the use of VAR in the Premier League may frighten a few people, but in fact this will likely end up being a very popular change, if executed correctly.

Since the introduction of VAR in 2019, the system was reserved for red cards, penalties and decisions leading to goals such as offsides and fouls. However, inspired by this summer's World Cup, Stockley Park’s help will now be in use for second yellow cards as well – a change that feels overdue.

VAR will also be taking a closer look at set-piece antics such as grappling and blocking, no doubt inspired by the controversy surrounding the number of goals scored from players flooding the six-yard box at corners and free kicks.

Extended time off the field for injured players

For years, we have seen players seemingly penalised for on-field injuries with a 30-second absence from the pitch after getting checked and being given the all-clear from their physios. But with suspicions that players are sometimes faking these injuries to waste time and disrupt the momentum of the game, Pro Ref will attempt to crack down on play-acting by extending the time penalty to one minute.

This could be a seismic change: with the surgical approach of so many modern coaches, being at a numerical disadvantage for up to a minute might prove catastrophic. But as with all these rules, we shall have to wait and see if they really do have the desired effect.

Timed substitutions

Again, this is another augmentation of an existing rule, with the aim of reducing time-wasting. For the last few seasons, players have been forced to leave the pitch at the closest possible exit point when substituted, rather than leisurely strolling over to the fourth official.

This rule will now be harsher on players, as they will have exactly 10 seconds to reach their exit point. If they fail to do so, the substitution will be delayed by a minimum of a minute and may be much longer at times, as they will have to wait for the next break in play. This means if a player fails to adhere to this new rule, their side could be a man down for some time.

The new rule has been specifically designed so players have no way round it, and surely now we might see the end of subs being made simply to waste time.

Handballs and pass-backs

This one is not so much a new rule but a statement of clarity from Pro Ref after some confusing and controversial moments from previous seasons.

With virtually every Premier League team employing short goal-kicks as opposed to an old-school punt up the field, we often see two centre halves stood either side of the goalkeeper in their own box. This has at times resulted in defenders picking up the ball, or accidentally performing a pass-back as it has been unclear if the ball is in play. In 2024, Arsenal’s Gabriel found himself in this situation in Champions League action against Bayern Munich, and narrowly escaped receiving a red card.

However, from next season onward an act like his will be punished. PGMOL have stated that as soon as the ball returns to the pitch and is distributed by the goalkeeper in any way play has resumed.

Tactical goalkeeper timeouts

Perhaps the most controversial change for the new season is a big one. In a meaningful trial this term, if the game is stopped for specifically a goalkeeper injury concern, the manager must immediately nominate an outfield player to leave the pitch.

Crucially, whichever player is selected must stay off the pitch for a minimum of one minute after the restart of play. Pro Ref has stated that the trial ‘is designed to address occasions where goalkeeper injuries have been used to disrupt momentum, slow the game down or create opportunities for tactical instruction.’

Gianluigi Donnarumma came under fire from Leeds manager Daniel Farke last season as he was accused to feigning injury to 'bend the rules'

Premier League fans will have found themselves increasingly frustrated by these ‘goalkeeper timeouts’ being used as an efficient form of gamesmanship in recent years, so this rule will have a very noticeable effect on players and managers.

And rules the Premier League has chosen to swerve...

Pro Ref have adopted some new rules that were implemented for the 2026 World Cup but not all of them. Some of the key omissions include:

VAR being used to review incorrectly awarded corners: While the top flight will give VAR a greater usage for fouls and second yellow cards, the scope is not extending to corners.

Red cards being given out for players covering their mouths: A contentious decision made by Pro Ref here. Due to the concerning amount of abuse players can give each other in the modern game, many footballing governing bodies seemed in favour of this rule to eradicate covert insults. One of the standout officiating moments of this summer's World Cup involved Miguel Almiron receiving the first red card for the gesture in Paraguay's colours. However, the Premier League believe that their current three-step discrimination protocol is sufficient.

Hydration breaks: Surely a universally agreed-upon positive decision.

'Mistaken identity'/yellows being reserved for diving: A more convoluted but still important clarification, as per International Football Association Board's ruling. A first yellow card can only be reviewed if the card is given to the wrong player, but the decision itself cannot be changed.

Sports.title: Axel Disasi closes in on Crystal Palace loan move as Chelsea continue their summer fire sale in attempt to trim Blues' bloated squad
Sports.content:
Axel Disasi is closing in on a loan move to Crystal Palace from Chelsea following talks.

It would see the 28-year-old Frenchman spend time with yet another Premier League club, after previously being loaned to Aston Villa and West Ham. The Hammers may have succeeded in signing him permanently this summer had they not been relegated to the Championship.

Negotiations between Palace and Chelsea have centred on a straightforward loan with no option or obligation. The Selhurst Park club will pay a fee and are expected to cover his wages if finalised.

Chelsea have already signed Maxence Lacroix from Palace in this window for £52million.

Disasi has been surplus to requirements at Stamford Bridge for some time, and has been training with the group separated from Xabi Alonso’s main squad at Cobham.

He impressed while on loan with West Ham last term despite them failing to avoid the drop.

Axel Disasi is set for yet another loan move with the Chelsea defender close to joining Palace

Disasi is unlikely to be the only centre back on his way out of Chelsea over the next week or so.

Benoit Badiashile is also in line to leave on a £3.4m loan to Napoli with a £23m option. Tosin Adarabioyo has interest from clubs in England and Europe, and Mamadou Sarr likewise has options.

Sports.title: Tottenham set to shatter £300m summer transfer spend after agreeing £85m deal with Manchester City for Savinho - and MORE arrivals are expected before window slams shut
Sports.content:
Tottenham set to shatter £300m summer transfer spend after agreeing £85m deal with Manchester City for Savinho - and MORE arrivals are expected before window slams shut

Tottenham have agreed a deal worth £85million for Manchester City winger Savinho.

The fee is £75m plus a further £10m in potential add-ons, a record sale for City.

Savinho's arrival will push Spurs' spending this summer past £300m, although they have recouped about £140m through the sales of Cristian Romero, Djed Spence and Luka Vuskovic.
