World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.title: What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.content:
What if the zombie apocalypse was already here?

In the late 2010s, Chinese indie band Hardcore Raver in Tears imagined just such a world in “Take Her to Wanda Plaza,” a jagged, synth-heavy sendup of the country’s mindless consumer culture. Over pounding beats, singer Lu Yan sang of zombified shoppers and took aim at Wang Sicong, the scion of the Wanda real estate empire and one of the most infamous of China’s “second-generation rich.”

The joke landed because Wanda Plaza is more than a shopping mall; by the 2010s, it had become shorthand for a particular vision of urban life. In the 2000s, local governments across the country saw real estate and urbanization as key engines of economic growth as well as fiscal revenue. Teaming with developers like Wanda, they built vast new tracts of standardized residential districts across the country. These new neighborhoods needed new stores and restaurants, a niche that Wanda also filled by building over 500 Wanda Plaza malls in more than 200 cities nationwide.

At the time, this was all taken for granted as modernization in action. China was urbanizing at a staggering speed, and clean, convenient, and air-conditioned shopping malls like Wanda Plaza were welcomed by both the country’s rising middle class and brands hungry to tap an emerging market.

But for the generation that came of age during this transformation, the convenience and prosperity of the new urban landscape is increasingly tinged with a sense of sameness. Rapid urban expansion did not just change how Chinese cities looked, they argue; it also displaced what anthropologist Xiang Biao calls the “nearby”: the small-scale places and relationships immediately around us through which everyday life acquires meaning.

That longing has since found an outlet online. From obsessively documenting faded Y2K architecture to creating virtual cities and nostalgic video games, young Chinese are attempting to recreate an idealized virtual version of the turn-of-the-millennium city: chaotic but colorful, and full of corner shops, wet markets, arcades, street stalls, and other places to hang out.

The most obvious example of this trend is Chinese dreamcore, which blends aspects of the global dreamcore subculture with elements drawn from China’s own millennial moment. The walking simulator “There Exists Nobody,” for example, invites players to revisit China’s bustling millennium-era towns, where neighborhoods were filled with unpolished mom-and-pop shops rather than sleek shopping malls.

A more sophisticated case is artist Huang Heshan’s digital metropolis “Too Rich City,” which he dubbed a work of “socialist cyberpunk.” Drawing on Huang’s experiences growing up in the southern province of Guangdong, the virtual city mixes modern LED screens with nostalgic elephant slides and swan-shaped boats — both recurring motifs in Chinese dreamcore.

Similarly, Liu Yujia, a photographer better known by his social media handle, “Tiehe West Street,” has built a large following for his dreamcore-style documentation of China’s long-maligned Y2K architecture.

When asked why his work resonates with so many, Huang commented that China’s millennial buildings — many of which have been allowed to fall into disrepair — nevertheless remain vibrant in ways the newer, more uniform apartment blocks aren’t. They’re “a little chaotic, but also more human,” he explained.

Indeed, a key motive of Chinese dreamcore is a desire for more human-scale spaces. Cookie-cutter blocks of shopping malls, chain stores, and gated residential communities have smoothed the rough edges of many Chinese cities, yet their lack of texture — places with which people can establish organic connections — has also led to widespread disorientation and disillusionment.

It is in this context that the “nearby,” the academic term popularized by Xiang, has entered public discourse in recent years. Rather than accepting the numbing comfort offered by places like Wanda Plaza, China’s younger generation is searching for informal spaces and trying to rebuild tight-knit communities.

Standardized urban planning, alongside an increasingly digital economy, has also reshaped people’s sense of time. In 2000, an ordinary Chinese person might experience time through walking to a grocery store, a school, or a park. Nowadays, such embodied experience has been replaced by the “estimated time of arrival” displayed in food delivery and car-hailing apps. This abstraction has rendered interpersonal relationships likewise abstract and fragile, contributing to the desire to return to a slower, less hectic era.

It’s worth noting that Chinese dreamcore is not the only space where the younger generation is seeking shelter and trying to build a digital “nearby.” The anime and fandom subcultures, for example, offer a similar sense of belonging.

Much of this can be traced back to worldwide trends like the loss of “third places” where young people can hang out away from parents and teachers, forcing them into online spaces increasingly divorced from their physical surroundings and leading to what the scholar Keith Hayward calls a culture of “self-infantilization” — such as the global social media craze for kitsch toys like Labubu.

It’s not hard to see why dreamcore-tinged nostalgia would find such fertile ground in both the West and China, even if one romanticizes malls while the other rejects them. These online trends have limits, however. Loosely organized, they lack the capability to make an impact offline. Meanwhile, some of the very offline spaces dreamcore fans like to criticize have effectively incorporated the subculture, positioning themselves as a new kind of “nearby.” Shopping hubs such as Shanghai’s Bailian mall and Beijing’s Wangfujing street now host regular events for anime fans, while Changsha’s Wenheyou has redecorated its commercial complexes to look like vintage markets and evoke feelings of “old Changsha.”

Ultimately, Y2K nostalgia is not immune to the consumerism it seeks to reject. With mounting financial pressure for commercial real estate developers, the Wanda Plaza model may have passed its heyday. Yet the urban landscape it has imposed upon us seems likely to last. They may complain about monotonous “new districts” and their lack of organic street life, but young Chinese continue to find the convenience that modern cities offer irresistible. Chinese dreamcore provides a temporary relief — sooner or later, though, we’re snapped awake by the buzz of our phones.

(Header image: 500px/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018906/China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.title: China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018906/China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.content:
When Wang Yijun walked out of the gaokao examination room on June 8, she immediately started thinking about what she’d do that summer. After three years of putting aside her hobbies and personal interests to study for China’s national college entrance exam, the 18-year-old from the eastern city of Wuxi finally had a summer of her own.

But the summer’s freedom came with a price tag. After the exam, Wang’s parents bought her a laptop costing over 10,000 yuan ($1,400), both as a reward for her years of effort and a tool for her future studies. She also traveled to Beijing and its neighboring city Tianjin, dined out with friends, and enrolled in an audio mixing course.

“I’ve spent around 20,000 yuan in total since the exam,” she told Sixth Tone in August.

Wang’s experience reflects a broader shift taking place across China. This summer — from the end of the exam to early September — students fresh out of the gaokao are splurging on electronics, graduation trips, and new hobbies before they have to buckle down at university.

For many, the spending can reach upwards of 40,000 yuan. For comparison, China’s per capita disposable income last year was 43,377 yuan.

This year, approximately 12.9 million students sat for the gaokao. A report jointly released by XKB Data Research Center and iiMedia Research estimated that incoming first-year students would spend an average of 18,600 yuan this summer, more than double compared with 2020. Spending by family members, such as on accompanying students on trips and celebratory meals, also ranged from 30,000 to 40,000 yuan. Together, the sector — termed the “post-gaokao economy” — is expected to surpass 387 billion yuan this year.

Merchants are moving quickly to seize the opportunity. Electronics sellers have launched promotions that give students special discounts when they present their gaokao admission tickets, while 327 top-rated scenic attractions across the country have rolled out concessions targeting the group. Cosmetic surgery clinics introduced student packages priced below 1,000 yuan, along with interest-free installment plans for customers who show their exam credentials.

But although the trend has provided a much-welcomed boost to the domestic economy, it has also sparked a growing generational debate over where celebration ends and excessive consumption begins. Posts by other young Chinese showing off their purchases, and sometimes sharing tricks to get their parents to buy things for them after the gaokao, soon began to spread online. And parents, facing financial pressure from their 18-year-olds, have now taken their complaints online.

A new coming-of-age ritual

The debate has fueled a popular online meme: “After all, you only finished the gaokao — you didn’t suddenly become rich,” capturing parental concerns over the post-exam consumption fever.

A screenshot of a mother’s chat messages reacting to her daughter’s post-exam shopping list — with items totaling more than 30,000 yuan — has also made the rounds on social media. In it, she says to her child, “How about you be my mom?”

For Chinese students, the summer after the gaokao carries a special significance. Longer than other school-time summers, it is widely considered the last extended break before adulthood brings a new set of pressures — from grad school applications and civil service exams to career choices.

“That makes it feel like a milestone worth celebrating,” Wang said.

On the last day of the gaokao, images of parents waiting outside examination halls with gifts for their children routinely flood domestic short-video platforms.

In one widely circulated video this year, students walked out of an exam room to find their parents holding stacks of laptops, smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, and earphones, jokingly referred to as quanjiatong, or a “bucket meal,” a reference to KFC’s all-in-one spread. Many such gift packages feature high-end brands such as Apple, with a full set costing north of 30,000 yuan.

Wang said her social media feed is now filled with posts by peers sharing graduation trips, unboxing new devices, and making plans to transform themselves during the break.

Seeing others mark the transition with new phones, designer products, and overseas travel, she added, has left many her age who have taken the gaokao but haven’t received or purchased such gifts feeling as though they are falling behind.

Coming from a working-class family, Wang said she tries to balance enjoyment with practicality. For instance, she decided to continue using her old phone because it still worked well.

“Families inevitably differ widely in their financial circumstances, and that’s a reality we cannot avoid,” she said. “If there is something we want, working for it ourselves is a sign of maturity.”

Before the gaokao, Wang added, grades provide a clear standard of achievement. “But once you walk out of that exam room, you’re suddenly surrounded by a world where people are judged by their material possessions. You start to believe that spending, having the latest gadgets, and traveling can fill the ‘void’ that comes with a major shift in identity.”

But, she added, “We’re not just ‘consumers.’ We can create, contribute, and slowly grow as people, which defines us far more than what we own.”

Greater costs

Qiu Jiqing, a professor of women’s studies and family relations at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Lifelong Education College, told Sixth Tone that when she took the gaokao in 1996, her experience was vastly different.

“My parents didn’t buy me any special gifts,” she said. “They simply prepared the necessities I would need for college. When I left for university, I basically took only my bedding and daily essentials with me.”

Qiu said she believes that spending within a family’s means after their child takes the gaokao is justified, especially in an era where electronic devices have become an essential part of education. However, she cautioned that social media and marketing campaigns could overly boost spending and desire for material goods among young people who are still developing their understanding of how and when to save and spend money.

“Learning to distinguish between what we truly need and what we simply want is part of growing up,” she said.

Regardless of whether or not they partake in gaokao celebratory splurging, for many families, the end of the exam marks the beginning of a new stage of spending.

Zhang Chunxing, a mother from the eastern Shandong province whose son took the gaokao this June, has already started calculating the costs of her son’s higher education.

She said that her son’s living costs will amount to around 18,000 yuan a year and tuition will add another 6,000 yuan annually. Transportation, accommodation, and other daily expenses will require additional investment.

“After the gaokao, many children want new phones, trips or other rewards,” she said. “But parents also have to think about the next four years.”

For Zhang, preparing for university is not only about covering costs, but also about teaching her son — who will be leaving home for the first time — how to manage his own expenses.

Qiu, the professor from Jiao Tong University, said that because students spend all their time and energy studying before the gaokao, other skills such as financial literacy, self-management, and independent living are often lacking.

She added that the transition is a challenge for the entire family, as most families are used to a dynamic where parents decide and children follow. After the gaokao, both must learn a new way of relating to each other.

“Students need to learn independence and parents also need to adjust to start seeing their children as individuals who can make their own decisions,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A teenager (right) receives a Nintendo Switch 2 from his older sister outside an exam site after the gaokao in Hefei, Anhui province, June 9, 2026. Han Suyuan/CNS/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018913/After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.title: After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018913/After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.content:
Chinese social media influencer Zhuge Yiyang, also known by her online alias Zhong Shu, has been accused of plagiarizing content across multiple podcast episodes and a Chinese article.

The allegations, which emerged last weekend on domestic social media, come just two weeks after she went viral for an interview with British-American director Christopher Nolan about his recent blockbuster “The Odyssey.”

The 29-year-old from eastern China’s Zhejiang province is currently a Ph.D. candidate in political philosophy at Boston College in the U.S. She also hosts the Chinese podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer,” which has over 970,000 subscribers on domestic podcast platform Xiaoyuzhou.

Her July 31 interview with Nolan in Beijing was viewed over 18 million times in an X post by video game journalist Geoff Keighley, the son of Nolan’s friend David Keighley.

Subsequent overseas media coverage of the interview — praised for Zhuge’s deeper philosophical questioning — brought her wider recognition on the Chinese internet, where many admired her prolific output, including podcast episodes released roughly every three days alongside her academic, translation, and writing work.

But that acclaim has been overshadowed by recent allegations that Zhuge used translated material from overseas podcasts, books, and magazines without attribution.

Among the allegations, her 310th podcast episode, released in March discussing Iran’s Islamic regime, was accused of plagiarizing an episode of the English-language podcast “Breaking History” released last August.

In the original episode, a guest mentions the establishment of both a health and literacy “corps,” which an AI-generated transcript on Apple Podcasts incorrectly renders as “court.” In her podcast, Zhuge similarly refers to them as “courts” in Chinese.

Social media users also pointed out that, beyond the use of “court,” the surrounding passages also closely overlap with the original podcast in both content and phrasing.

Users also accused Zhuge of plagiarizing a May article in The Atlantic on university students’ use of AI in a similar column she wrote in August for Chinese business news outlet Caixin.

Among the similarities, the first paragraphs of both articles cite the same line from Princeton University’s student newspaper. Zhuge’s second paragraph also describes the university’s honor code as having “lasted through two world wars, the upheaval of the 1960s, the disillusionment of Watergate, and even the rise of search engines” — a line from the third paragraph of the Atlantic article.

In an interview with domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily published on Monday, Zhuge responded to the allegations only by saying, “We live in an age that demands apologies from greatness,” a line she had used in her interview with Nolan. She did not elaborate on how the remark related to the allegations.

In her 364th podcast episode, released the same day, Zhuge said that when she first began podcasting, her life in the U.S. was “a mess” while people in China had been “quite friendly.”

“Now the situation has completely reversed,” she said without elaborating.

Zhuge also said in the episode that she had plans to appear on “a whole bunch of podcasts by Western intellectuals.” She added that American intellectuals also routinely face intense criticism online, citing American political scientist Francis Fukuyama as an example.

The same day, three August book talks Zhuge was scheduled to attend in Shanghai and the central Hubei and Hunan provinces to promote her recent translations of works by German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt were also canceled, with the organizer citing “changes to (Zhuge’s) personal schedule.”

Sixth Tone contacted Zhuge multiple times for comment on the controversy through her publicly listed personal email address, but received no response.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG and Bilibili, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.title: Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.content:
Poorly animated yellow cows walking on two legs, raw voice acting, and extremely slow pace — these are characteristics of China’s most recent box office hit and viral phenomenon.

Released Aug. 5 after virtually no promotion, the movie, “Niu Lai,” or “Cow Comes,” is named for its titular character: a calf who struggles to stand. The film follows Niu Lai and his herd as they overcome a number of difficulties while migrating, eventually growing up into an able-bodied adult cow unfazed in the face of danger. Except, Niu Lai awakens, realizing that he is still a calf — but he is finally able to support his own weight.

The movie, reported to have no financial backing, earned just 5,500 yuan ($815) at the box office in its first week. But after multiple viewers posted images of the film on social media criticizing it, that number suddenly surged to over 710,000 yuan on Aug. 15, according to ticketing platform Maoyan. As of Tuesday afternoon, it has taken in 20 million yuan, a figure projected to grow to 135 million yuan by the time it leaves screens.

The reason for its explosive popularity? Its absurdist visuals and overall crude production design have turned it into a word-of-mouth viral phenomenon. The characters’ legs rarely move in sync, making them appear like they’re sliding. Close-ups of their heads are overblown and blurry. Transitions between scenes are jarring and illogical, and the characters’ voices are poorly recorded and overly stilted.

The effect has led to highly polarized ratings on domestic review platform Douban, with many giving it either one or five stars. As one highly upvoted comment on Maoyan reads, “You don’t have to watch bad movies, but when a movie is bad enough, you have to.”

Wang Yunfei, the founder of a cartoon studio and an acting animated film judge at various film festivals, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper, “Professional animators couldn’t produce something this poorly even if they made mistakes. So from a professional standpoint, there’s really nothing to critique. It’s just spectacle-watching.”

The movie’s unexpectedly raw, homemade production has also been regarded by critics and viewers alike as a rebuke to high-investment but poorly reviewed films.

“Niu Lai” was produced by Jingyuan Culture Film and Television Media, based in the northeastern city of Dalian, which was converted from a one-person renovation company, according to corporate data platform Qichacha.

The renovator in question is the film’s creator, 34-year-old Xin Yumeng, who made it alongside his mother, Sun Lifang. The pair reportedly had no background in animation and made the film over five years, without the help of AI. They also provided the voices for the characters, while Sun composed and sang the film’s theme song.

On a domestic radio show, Xin said that he made the film out of a love for animated films, and chose a cow as the protagonist because his father was born in the Year of the Ox.

As for the quality of the film, Xin added that much of the equipment he bought secondhand for the film’s production eventually broke down. “Even the computer motherboards burned out ... The final result has a lot to do with the equipment used.”

Le Fumin, a 35-year-old security worker from Shanghai, told domestic media that he liked that “Niu Lai” was made by two ordinary people, rather than having large film-industry backing. “It shows a bit of rebellion against the assembly-line formula of mainstream filmmaking,” he said. “Why should I only be allowed to watch what the industry feeds me? The kind of happiness I choose for myself is worth the ticket price, too.”

Le said the atmosphere in the theater was particularly relaxed. “Over the course of two hours, the pressure of meeting KPIs at work, the exhaustion of commuting, and all the troubles of everyday life just melted away with the laughter of the whole theater,” he said. “It felt like returning to something simple and genuine — like the carefree feeling of watching random films in a video rental shop as a kid.”

As “Niu Lai” has risen in popularity, fan-made tributes to it have spread online and offline, with some placing Niu Lai into posters for recent international box office hits such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey.” Cinema staff have also put up rudimentary, hand-drawn posters advertising the film — and paying homage to its crude animation — outside theaters.

Even stocks of three companies with “niu” in their names — Jinniu Chemical Industry, Goneo Group, and Tongniu Information — shot into the top five trending list on domestic finance data platform Tonghuashun over the weekend, as the film’s title can be interpreted as “the bull market is coming,” domestic media reported.

Other entities are also capitalizing on the film’s virality, creating their own animal-based animated shorts to promote products. On Monday, local authorities for Dongguan City in the southern Guangdong province produced a video titled “E Lai,” or “Goose Comes,” to promote the city’s local specialty — roast goose — garnering more than 26,000 likes on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

For most, however, the movie is simply about having fun. Mak SzeNing, a 27-year-old pet care worker from Hong Kong, watched the film in the eastern city of Hangzhou at a nearly sold-out screening. “I don’t think the movie’s value lies in its production quality,” she told Sixth Tone. “Its value is that it brings a group of strangers into the same theater, and suddenly everyone feels like they’ve found their kindred spirits and laughs together.”

“If a movie can make people laugh, then I think it’s a good movie,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Niu Lai.” From Douban)

World.title: China Tests Pausing Countdowns for Delivery Riders at Red Lights
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018898/China Tests Pausing Countdowns for Delivery Riders at Red Lights
World.content:
Multiple Chinese cities are implementing a new timer system for delivery riders that factors in the time spent stopped at red lights, easing how long they have to get items to customers.

The system was announced on Aug. 13 by delivery platforms Taobao Flash, JD Food Delivery, and Meituan at a meeting in Beijing with authorities from both Beijing and Shanghai, as well as experts and lawmakers to discuss changes to existing delivery rules.

The same day, Meituan announced the pilot of the system in Beijing, which went into effect in Beijing’s Chaoyang and Tongzhou districts and the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, in the city’s suburb of Yizhuang. Suzhou in the eastern Jiangsu province also began a pilot of the system on both Meituan and Taobao Flash on July 31.

Delivery of food, goods, and special packages in China is a race against the clock, with riders granted little time to complete each order. When a customer places an order via a delivery app, it is transferred to riders, who then choose whether or not to accept it. Platforms require orders to be delivered within a certain time; otherwise, riders incur a penalty.

Before implementing the new system, delivery apps calculated the entire time from order acceptance to a package’s successful delivery, not factoring in the time riders spent stopped at traffic lights. This led to a culture of delivery riders running red lights to make their deliveries on time.

According to a video Meituan released the same day as the announcement, when riders stop at a red light, the app’s delivery page will display a countdown timer for when the light will turn green. A pop-up message from its AI safety assistant then informs them, “Stop at the red light. We’re recording the waiting time. The delivery time for this order will be extended when it ends.”

Once the delivery is completed, the app displays the order number, cumulative time spent at red lights, and a recalculated permissible delivery time based on that figure.

Meituan told Sixth Tone on Monday that it previously estimated time riders spent at red lights based on offline data and algorithmic prediction — a less precise method for e-bikes. With the new system, however, the platform calculates time spent at red lights by accessing real-time traffic light data from traffic management departments, combined with the rider’s location, direction of travel, and delivery route — information provided by the Meituan app.

The new rules will also change how other factors affect delivery time. For example, platforms will extend delivery times if an order is transferred between riders or if adverse weather and difficult road conditions occur. Orders that are delayed at the point of preparation will not influence a rider’s service score.

The estimated time shown to customers will also be adjusted in real time to reduce pressure on riders, using an average speed of no more than 15 kilometers per hour to calculate arrival time.

Li Yipeng, a food-delivery rider in Suzhou, told domestic media, “Now we can clearly see how long we waited at the red light and how much extra time we were given. As riders, we don’t need to worry anymore, and we definitely won’t have to run red lights anymore.”

On Aug. 17, Meituan announced that the system would immediately go into effect in the city of Wuxi in Jiangsu province. The same day, Taobao Flash also told Sixth Tone that the system went into effect today in the eastern city of Qingdao.

Meituan also told domestic media that it is currently reviewing more than 20 other cities as possible extensions of the policy’s scope, and expects it to cover more than 1 million riders by the end of the year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: FACT CHECK: UPLIFT program does not offer P5,000 cash aid, rice subsidy to all Filipinos
World.content:
The misleading post circulating online is one of several that promise cash aid to registered individuals. Contrary to the claim, only eligible sectors qualify for the cash assistance.

Claim: All Filipinos, including those not included in the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps), can receive a sack of rice and P5,000 in cash assistance upon registering for the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) program.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook page named “Uplift News and Updates” published two videos of a female news anchor announcing a rice subsidy and cash aid for all Filipinos.

The two posts garnered a total of 4,200 likes, 1,800 comments, and 1,970 shares as of writing.

The supposed news anchor said, “Lahat ng Pilipino, kahit hindi 4Ps member, ay makakakuha ng isang sakong bigas at P5,000. Ang payout ay sa August 22, 2026. Ang registration ay makikita dito sa post namin at sa comment section.”

(All Filipinos, even non-4Ps members, will receive a sack of rice and P5,000. The payout is scheduled for August 22, 2026. Registration details can be found in this post and in the comment section.)

Viewers are then directed to links to register for the supposed payout.

The facts: Contrary to the claim, cash aid through the UPLIFT program is only given to eligible beneficiaries, not to all Filipinos.

The UPLIFT program, implemented by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), is intended to protect vulnerable sectors from falling further into poverty due to the effects of the energy emergency caused by the Middle East conflict. It provides cash aid only to eligible predetermined beneficiaries. Filipinos do not need to register for the program, according to the social welfare department.

The DSWD began a fresh round of cash aid rollout on July 21, with beneficiaries classified into three groups:

Group 1 – 3.5 million families enrolled in the DSWD’s 4Ps and the Walang Gutom Program

Group 2 – 2.5 million households not enrolled in 4Ps, but classified as poor and near-poor based on the Community-Based Monitoring System of the Philippine Statistics Authority

Group 3 – 1.5 million low-income workers and their families who are eligible members of the Social Security System

Those under Group 1 will receive a one-time subsidy of P2,000, while beneficiaries under Groups 2 and 3 will receive P2,000 per month from July to December 2026.

Furthermore, the “Uplift News and Updates” page is not affiliated with the DSWD. The social welfare department has repeatedly reminded the public to be wary of potential scams and rely only on its official channels for legitimate updates.

AI-generated: AI detection tool SightEngine flagged a screenshot of the video as 99% likely to be AI-generated. HiveDetect said the whole video is 62.9% likely to be AI-generated.

Link scanner urlscan.io showed that the links in the caption direct users to a form that asks for their full name, age, sex, and address. It classified the links as malicious. Users who provide their information through these forms risk falling victim to phishing scams. (READ: Phishing 101: How to spot and avoid phishing)

Previous fact checks: Rappler has debunked similar fake government assistance videos claiming to provide cash aid and subsidies:

– Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Chog Moral shines, but Gilas Boys still fall to China in U18 Asia Cup
World.content:
Pampanga pride Chog Moral turns in his best performance in a Gilas Boys uniform, albeit in a quarterfinal loss to China that denies the Philippines a seat in the 2027 FIBA U19 World Cup

MANILA, Philippines – Rising star Chog Moral played the game of his life, but Gilas Boys still fell short in taking down powerhouse China, suffering a 117-103 loss in the quarterfinals of the FIBA U18 Asia Cup in Ahmedabad, India, on Friday, August 21.

The 18-year-old from Pampanga fired a game-high 26 points to go with 6 steals and 2 rebounds in the loss that denied the Philippines a seat in the 2027 FIBA U19 World Cup in the Czech Republic.

Averaging just 6.3 points in the first four games, Moral waxed hot this time, shooting an efficient 10-of-14 clip and scattering 19 points in the second half, although the Chinese hardly felt any resistance as they preserved their double-digit lead until the end.

Moral converted on a free throw and a layup in succession to pull Gilas Boys within 91-106 with under two minutes remaining before China answered with 5 straight points to seal the victory.

Four more players scored in double figures for the Philippines, with Luke Edward Atacador firing 14 points, Ethan Aguas and JB Cagurungan adding 12 points each, and George Green contributing 11 points and 5 rebounds.

Wang Zichao and Chen Yuxiu posted 25 and 23 points, respectively, to pace China, which led from the get-go after mounting a 33-20 advantage at end of the opening quarter.

The Philippines missed out on a return to the U19 World Cup for the first time since current Gilas Pilipinas mainstays Kai Sotto, AJ Edu, and Carl Tamayo represented the country in the 2019 edition as only the top four teams will qualify for the global hoops showdown.

Relegated to the classification phase, Gilas Boys can still finish as high as fifth. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Newsstand] Covering an apartheid state committing genocide
World.content:
I will start with the fundamental facts in the year 2026: Israel is an apartheid state. It is committing genocide in Palestine. And it has killed over 200 journalists in Gaza.

That horrifying sum is higher, according to the Costs of War Project in Brown University, than the total number of journalists killed in World War I, World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War and the other wars in Indochina, the wars in the former Yugoslavia, and the US war in Afghanistan…combined. (Here’s a link to a summary and to the full paper.)

Let me add one more fact: International public opinion about Israel has turned markedly negative, likely because many now perceive it as an apartheid regime, running a relentless campaign of genocide in the Gaza Strip (and encouraging settler violence in the West Bank). The 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that, even in the Philippines, 64% of the population held unfavorable views of Israel.

In the controversy over the press visit organized in August by the Israeli government for Filipino journalists, this is my starting point. These are my premises. The press visit is a deliberate and disciplined attempt, by a determined and extremely capable government, to counter the negative perceptions about the state it represents. Negative but accurate, because Israel does run an institutionalized system of segregation and discrimination against Palestinians in occupied territory and even in Israel itself, and because Israel does continue to wage an organized and ruthless campaign (visible through the partial but still graphic view seen on media and on social media) to destroy Palestine and its people in Gaza.

Negative, accurate — and for many, including myself, belated. (I used to be such a fervent supporter of “the only democracy in the Middle East.”)

Under these atrocious conditions, why would a journalist accept an invitation from the genocidal apartheid regime to, in the words of the Israeli embassy’s Facebook post, “experience Israel beyond the headlines, through meaningful conversations, cultural exchanges, and firsthand encounters”?

On the ground

The post is written in the key of normalcy; it’s just another country inviting foreign journalists to see life as it is really lived back home. And, to be completely fair, many on social media read and received it that way. After all, wouldn’t it be better if Filipino journalists actually have on-the-ground experience in Israel? Shouldn’t Israel be allowed, like other countries, to make its case before the world? And doesn’t the real test of journalistic independence from Israeli government control come later, when the stories run?

The press visit has stirred a controversy, and not only among journalists. Among my colleagues in the profession, the issue has become especially contentious. To be sure, there is an imbalance in the forces; organizations such as the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines have issued statements condemning the press visit; no institution related to journalism has issued a defense.

But there is also this: some members of the institutions that criticized the visit expressed some uncertainty in private about whether the lines were in fact that clear-cut, or whether other, previous press visits would be able to meet today’s severe test. Still others have noted, or mocked, the moralistic tone of much of the criticism.

I believe it is still possible to engage in a good-faith discussion of the issue. When I invited Palawan News editor in chief Dempto Anda, a former colleague from the Inquirer for whom I have great respect and one of the 19 journalists who went on the press visit, to discuss the controversy on the Media Nation on Air program on Radyo Katipunan, I told him at the outset (because I wanted to be upfront) that I thought he was wrong to go, but assured him that I and my other co-hosts were committed to an open and fair conversation.

What are the possible reasons for accepting the Israeli government’s invitation? I can discern at least four arguments that justify the press visit.

“It’s called public diplomacy. Everyone does it.”

Press visits are a fact of life. States, corporations, foundations all do it — even today, even given the highly fragmented media landscape, even with trust ratings for the news media brought deliberately low by targeted criticism and politically sponsored demonization. Original, independent reporting still carries real weight. Even rebel movements adjust to it. “When you’re allowed entry sa isang NPA camp, hindi ba curated experience din ’yun?,” someone with decades of experience in journalism asks. Another veteran journalist says: “Every so often we are in similar situations. Common ang sponsored trips, sponsored this, sponsored that. Making an ethical decision in one does not make you ethical for life.”

“Others have committed war crimes and genocide too.”

This is the line of argument of friends like lawyer (and former journalist) Romel Regalado Bagares, who asks: “How about journalists doing US-sponsored fellowships (if we follow the argument that the US is the world’s biggest sponsor of war crimes and genocides)?” Replying to Bagares, acclaimed documentary filmmaker Howie Severino offers a nuanced take that I believe is still sympathetic to Bagares’ view. “I was a Chevening scholar in the UK, all expenses paid by the British government, which colonized much of the world and even occupied parts of the Philippines for over a year. It didn’t come with a condition to be nice to them in my future coverage. But did my deeper understanding of their culture and history make me more sympathetic?”

“You’re being given access to a place that’s hard to go to.”

This third argument, best expressed on Facebook by Straits Times editor (and former Inquirer colleague) Raul Dancel, can be summed up in one word: access. “The way I see it, you are being offered access to a place that is normally shut to someone like you, and, any journalist worth his/her/their salt knows that access is one of the currencies of journalism: It is what gets you your story.” Then he adds: “What you do with your access is another matter entirely.”

“Judge us by our stories.”

This approach, if I understand Anda correctly, is his main argument. He replies to criticism from Inday Espina Varona, another colleague and for many a spirit guide in journalism, first by acknowledging that her questions are fair (“You’re not wrong to ask”) and then, referring to the principle that genuine press freedom requires working without fear or censorship, offers a pledge: “I think it’s the standard we should be judged against when the pieces come out.”

This is an argument that Bagares and Dancel also support. “That’s the point about this vilification of journalists joining a ‘ junket.’ Wala pa reportage eh,” Bagares says. “The proof is in the story you write, not in your attendance,” Dancel says. “Complicity is a choice.”

Bagares provided a photo collage of books written by “people who took ‘junkets’ and made the most of them” — to reinforce the point. But, as I argued in my reply to his post, he was stretching the meaning of the word “junket” to its breaking point. The writers he pointed to may have enjoyed a government-funded freebie or two (riding a US Army helicopter in Vietnam, stowing away on an American hospital ship on D-Day), but to argue that Martha Gellhorn or Philip Knightley or Jonathan Schell benefited from a curated experience “beyond the headlines” that is convenient by design (scheduled meetings, special transportation arrangements, sponsored meals, etc) is to misrepresent their work.

Fact of life

In general terms, I agree with the four arguments. Press visits are a fact of newsroom life. These may be the only way chronically underfunded newsrooms can send their journalists to do overseas reporting. As long as no constraints are placed on the stories themselves, it’s a practice that can be tolerated or (as I did when I was editor in chief of Inquirer.net) even encouraged.

And journalists who join press visits should be evaluated by the stories they file too. Sometimes a sympathetic view cannot be avoided, but even then a story or an analysis can still manage to be original, complex rather than simplistic, bound to truth rather than propaganda. Access is a currency, and the opportunity to get close to or even to get into a conflict zone is compelling for many reasons. And it is true that many of the governments that sponsor press visits have or have had blood on their hands; indeed, for some of them, that they are in a position to sponsor these visits is directly linked to the violence they had earlier inflicted on other places.

But these four arguments rely on two shared assumptions that we should seriously and severely question.

The first assumption, on which the first two arguments depend, is the notion that there’s no real difference between the Israel committing genocide now and, say, the British at the turn of the 20th century who imprisoned the Boers in concentration camps and caused the deaths of tens of thousands. Or between going on the Israeli press visit this month and, say, accepting an International Visitor Leadership Program nomination from the US Department of State today. If there is a difference, it is only one of degree.

I think, however, that in fact the difference is one of kind. Israel is committing genocide right this minute, even during a so-called ceasefire. And despite the targeted killings of mainly Palestinian journalists, the partial evidence available on media and social media is vivid, detailed, and unequivocal. This is the first genocide broadcast live around the world; there has been nothing like it in history. And it is precisely because of its impact on international public opinion that press visits like the one conducted this month have been organized. “Experience Israel beyond the headlines” eventually leads to “let’s talk about anything, except headline news about apartheid and genocide.”

Again, the destruction of Palestine is ongoing. Did the Dutch colonial government, to give only one example, organize press tours during the Indonesian war of independence, when Dutch troops massacred thousands? But here we have the Israeli government doing exactly that while the killings are going on. What, not even a temporary cessation for the benefit of visiting observers?

A comparison between “Reported Impact Snapshots” prepared by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs for August 5 and for August 12, roughly the same time as the press visit, shows that seven Palestinians were reported killed and 28 recorded as sustaining injuries in that week alone. The total number of killed, as of August 12, stands at 73,388. (Also, the OCHA count for the number of journalists killed is 262.)

The second shared assumption, on which the last two arguments rely, is the idea that — despite the best efforts of a highly capable government to wring propaganda value out of a press visit — the individual journalist will still find a way to find, write, and publish stories or analyses that criticize the Israeli policy on apartheid, the Israeli case for genocide. I mean, that must be what “judge us by our stories” mean, right, in this particular context?

But now an unwelcome calculus: How many such critical stories should we expect from the 19 journalists who went to Israel? At least one per journalist? Or just one for the entire delegation? This may seem like nitpicking, but as even Dancel says, the visit “seems like an exercise in sly propaganda.” How many critical stories are needed, then, to justify taking on the reputational risk? What if someone were a lifestyle journalist; would we expect him to write on the extermination of a people? And if one such story does raise the supposed debate over how to describe what is happening in Gaza — a debate favorable to the Israeli government — should it also mention that International Court of Justice judges, United Nations experts, genocide scholars, and even Israeli human rights groups have called the tragedy in Gaza a genocide?

And what can the delegates do, when the Israeli government uses them — not their stories, but the fact of their participation in a seemingly normal press visit, their mere attendance — to drive home the message of normalcy? Complicity is a choice, yes, but the choosing begins well before the stories are even written. – Rappler.com

Veteran journalist John Nery is a Rappler columnist. He anchors Rappler’s special coverage of the Duterte impeachment trial and, every Wednesday, hosts In the Public Square with John Nery. Full disclosure: He has taken part in government-sponsored press visits, including China in 2008, Singapore in 2013, and France in 2015, 2016, and 2018. Many of the stories and all of the columns that came out of these visits are on his Newsstand blog.

World.title: Want to install solar panels? How DOE’s simplified rules apply to you
World.content:
The Department of Energy's new rules cover solar systems meant primarily for the consumer's own electricity use rather than for selling power back to the grid under a net-metering program

MANILA, Philippines – Filipinos who want to install solar panels to ease their electricity bills may now have less paperwork to deal with, but exactly how simple the process becomes depends on what kind of system they install.

The Department of Energy’s (DOE) new rules cover solar systems meant primarily for the consumer’s own electricity use rather than for selling power back to the grid under a net-metering program. But within that broad category are three different setups, each with its own requirements: connected zero-export systems, isolated zero-export systems, and small micro-solar systems (MSS).

The biggest change is that distribution utilities such as Meralco and electric cooperatives can no longer require pre-installation clearances, technical permits, or inspection fees as a condition for installing systems covered by the policy. Utilities may still study how installations affect their networks, but must shoulder the cost themselves and cannot use the study to delay or block installation.

Which rules apply to you?

The easiest category is an MSS, which are small, consumer-grade or plug-and-play setup.

To qualify, the solar panels must have a total capacity of no more than 1 kilowatt (kW), paired with a micro-inverter with a maximum output of 0.8 kW. The system must also meet electrical and safety requirements. (READ: What will it take for solar power to take off in the Philippines?)

For consumers installing an MSS, they simply need to notify their distribution utility — such as Meralco — using the DOE’s prescribed form. No building permit or Certificate of Compliance (COC) from the Energy Regulatory Commission is required under the circular.

Consumers with analog meters also don’t have to wait for a meter replacement before installation. The utility has up to 12 months after notification to replace the meter with one suitable for MSS installations, while the existing meter may continue to be used temporarily.

Those with larger solar installations fall under what the DOE calls Self-Generating Facility Zero-Export Solar Systems (SGF ZESS). Unlike an MSS, there is no capacity ceiling, but the system must be configured so that electricity is not exported to the distribution grid.

There are two kinds: connected SGF ZESS and isolated SGF ZESS.

SIMPLIFIED. Table of requirements for each type of solar system. DOE Department Circular 2026-08-0017.

A connected SGF ZESS remains connected to the distribution system but uses equipment that prevents excess solar electricity from flowing into the grid. Consumers installing one must notify their distribution utility and secure a building permit.

A completely isolated SGF ZESS, meanwhile, operates independently from the distribution grid. No notification to the utility is required, but a building permit still is.

While both connected and isolated SGF ZESS require a building permit, consumers may not have to get a new one if their local government verifies that an existing building permit is sufficient for the solar installation.

The COC requirement depends on who will use the system. Households, clinics, hospitals, and other medical facilities are exempt from securing a COC for SGF ZESS installations. Other users, such as businesses, generally still need one.

And if you’re hoping to earn from the excess electricity your solar panels generate, these streamlined rules are not for you. Any electricity sent back to the grid under these arrangements will not earn bill credits or payments.

To receive credits for excess solar power, consumers still have to enroll in the net-metering program and enter into a net-metering agreement with their distribution utility, which are goverened by a different set of paperwork requirements.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the policy is intended to remove costs and requirements that can discourage consumers from adopting solar in the first place.

“By simplifying the process and removing unnecessary costs and requirements, we are opening the door for more households, clinics, and small businesses to generate clean electricity for their own use,” Garin said.

According to the Department of Energy, the measure is meant to directly support the energy directive of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in his 2026 State of the Nation Address. Marcos had called for faster renewable energy adoption and for rooftop solar and battery storage installation to become simpler and more affordable.

The Philippines currently gets 25% of its energy from renewables and hopes to reach a renewable energy target of 35% of the power generation mix by 2030 and 50% by 2040. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No DepEd announcement abolishing Grades 11 and 12
World.content:
The Department of Education has repeatedly debunked false information on the supposed removal of the K to 12 program

Claim: The Department of Education (DepEd) announced that Grades 11 and 12 will be abolished starting June 2027.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook account posted a series of graphics with the claim on August 17 and 18. The post incorporated the official DepEd logo.

It also included the caption, “Good news talaga. K-12 no more,” along with a link where readers can supposedly find the list of affected schools and the source of the claim.

As of writing, the series of posts have accumulated 139 reactions, 35 comments, and 234 shares.

The facts: The announcement is fake. There are no official reports or advisories from DepEd stating that Grades 11 and 12 will be removed starting next academic year. The K to 12 program remains in effect as it is mandated by law under the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013.

On March 14, DepEd debunked a similar claim alleging the removal of the K to 12 program for the current academic year. The department advised the public to refer exclusively to its official channels for announcements and verified information regarding basic education.

K to 12 debates: While claims on social media regarding the supposed removal of the K to 12 program are fake, discussions on revising or removing senior high school have resurfaced in Congress.

In June 2025, Senator Jinggoy Estrada filed Senate Bill No. 3001 or the proposed Rationalized Basic Education Act. The bill seeks to remove senior high school and restore a four-year secondary education system. In the same year, DepEd launched its pilot implementation of the revised K to 12 senior high school curriculum, which reduces core subjects for Grade 11 students and simplifies educational tracks amid ongoing questions regarding the program’s effectiveness.

In August 2026, Republic Act No. 12322 amended Republic Act No. 10533 to remove the mandatory requirement for the “spiral progression” approach. The new law gives DepEd the flexibility to adopt whichever teaching methods it deems most effective for learners. (READ: What removal of mandatory ‘spiral progression’ means for K to 12 program)

Suspicious links: The misleading post provided no evidence to support its claim. Instead, it included links to supposed official announcements, claiming that the list of affected schools and the source article could be accessed through them. The post even used a URL containing terms like “list-areas” and “DepEd-article” to appear legitimate. A closer look at the links reveals that they redirect to an unrelated online shopping website.

Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked false claims about the removal of the K to 12 program:

– Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is journalist based in Bicol and Baguio, and an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Volunteer Portal Proposal Could Turn Global Initiative Into Practical Tool
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s proposed international volunteer portal could be more than an image project, giving the country an opportunity to turn its global volunteer agenda into a practical mechanism for international cooperation, said an expert with the National Volunteer Network.

“If the initiative is implemented, for our country this will be much more than an image project. It is an opportunity to establish the role of a country that not only supports volunteering domestically, but also proposes concrete mechanisms for its development at the global level,” Aiman Nakispekova, coordinator of the International Volunteer Center at the National Volunteer Network, told The Astana Times.

From initiative to practical mechanism

Kazakhstan proposed creating a unified international portal to register volunteers, determine their status and systematize areas of activity during a meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Culture and Information Aida Balayeva and UN Volunteers Executive Coordinator Toily Kurbanov on Aug. 19.

The proposal follows Kazakhstan’s initiative to proclaim 2026 the International Year of Volunteers for Sustainable Development, endorsed by the UN General Assembly.

On Aug. 20, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Kurbanov to discuss Kazakhstan’s role in advancing the global volunteer agenda. Tokayev said more than 1,000 events are being held in Kazakhstan during the year, while the number of volunteers has approached 300,000. Kazakhstan is also developing a volunteer movement concept through 2030 and introducing a digital volunteer passport.

Nakispekova sees the portal as a logical continuation of these efforts, moving Kazakhstan from a political initiative toward a practical international tool. She stressed that it should not necessarily be viewed as a new institution created by Kazakhstan, but as international volunteering infrastructure developed with its support and participation.

What could make it different?

International volunteering already has digital infrastructure. UN Volunteers operates a Unified Volunteering Platform where candidates create profiles and apply for assignments within the UN system.

Kazakhstan’s proposal could add value by going beyond UN recruitment and connecting national volunteer organizations, volunteers and projects across countries.

Kazakhstan already has relevant domestic experience. Its Qazvolunteer platform connects volunteers, organizations and projects and includes opportunities for volunteering abroad. An international model could build on this experience while accommodating different national systems and local priorities.

The system behind the platform

The portal’s value would ultimately depend on the infrastructure supporting it.

Tatyana-Tinkay Koreshkova, an expert with the National Volunteer Network, said the priority should be coordination and verification.

“For this to work well, what is needed is not so much a website or portal as a powerful back office,” she told The Astana Times.

Such a system would need to verify volunteers and opportunities, connect organizations, support safety and coordinate logistics. This would require sustained cooperation among participating countries and organizations.

What Kazakhstan could gain

For Kazakhstan, the initiative could strengthen its international profile while giving practical substance to its leadership in the

global volunteer agenda. A functioning system could also facilitate the exchange of experience, increase the visibility of volunteer contributions and strengthen cross-border civil-society cooperation.

The main test will be implementation, including common approaches to verification, coordination, safety, financing and measuring results.

During Kurbanov’s meeting with Kazakh Minister of Foreign Affairs Yermek Kosherbayev on Aug. 19, the officials discussed expanding Kazakh volunteers’ participation in UN activities and promoting Kazakhstan’s experience in volunteering internationally. They also discussed developing the volunteer agenda beyond 2026 at the national, regional and international levels.

If these mechanisms are developed, Kazakhstan could move from promoting volunteering as a global priority to helping build practical infrastructure for cross-border volunteer cooperation.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Reforms, Investment and Regional Role
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles on Kazakhstan featured in international media worldwide this week. Today’s foreign media digest covers Kazakhstan’s AI education initiatives, political reforms and upcoming Kurultai election, investment prospects, and growing role in Central Asian and Eurasian cooperation.

Kazakhstan rolls out AI education from school to university

In the 2026-27 academic year, Kazakhstan’s first artificial intelligence university plans to enroll 600 students and trainees. AI use is also being expanded in schools, with a separate pilot planned for ten small rural schools. Kazakhstan is therefore trying to build its AI talent pipeline from both ends of the education system, reported The Times of Central Asia on Aug. 18.

Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek announced the first intake at Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU) during a government meeting.

Nurbek said 400 students would be admitted to bachelor’s programs, including 308 on state grants, while another 100 would join master’s programs.

“In addition, the Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund will send 100 of its employees to study under the MBA AI+X program,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s next chapter: Reform, resilience, and partnership with Europe

EU Reporter published an article on Aug. 18 by Roman Vassilenko, Kazakhstan’s ambassador to Belgium, highlighting Kazakhstan’s political reforms, economic resilience, strategic importance in energy and transport, and growing partnership with the European Union.

“On 23 August, Kazakhstan will hold its first elections to the Kurultai, the new highest representative body established under our new Constitution. The elections represent an important stage in the political modernization and the building of a Just Kazakhstan initiated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The new Kurultai and the elections to it are part of a broader effort to strengthen representative institutions, widen political participation and build a more resilient political system. A total of seven political parties compete in the elections, seeking to clear the 5% threshold.

As a Kazakh saying goes, ‘Where there is unity, there is strength.’ For us, the strength of a modern state rests not only on economic performance, but also on effective institutions, public participation and confidence in the future.

As we approach this critical milestone, it is important to put it in a broader geopolitical context, including our cooperation with the world and with the European Union,” reads the article.

Investment outlook for Kazakhstan equities: Strategic allocation to Eurasia’s hidden blue-chip market

EU Reporter published an article by Rainer Michael Preiss, Partner & Portfolio Strategist at Das Family Office in Singapore on Aug. 18, highlighting Kazakhstan as an under-owned but increasingly attractive investment market, citing its strong economic growth, competitive valuations, robust banking sector, strategic position in uranium, energy and the Middle Corridor, and ongoing economic reforms while acknowledging risks such as commodity-price volatility, geopolitical uncertainty and market liquidity.

The article argues that Kazakhstan offers global investors and family offices a compelling long-term diversification opportunity beyond traditional developed and emerging markets. It highlights the country’s expected GDP growth of around 4-4.5%, strong performance of the tenge and domestic equities, leadership in uranium production, growing logistics and financial sectors, and improving institutional and corporate governance. While recognizing risks linked to commodities, geopolitics, currency movements and market liquidity, the author concludes that Kazakhstan’s attractive valuations, strong financial institutions, strategic resources and economic reforms support a BUY recommendation for Kazakhstan equities as a strategic long-term allocation.

Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyz Republic’s multidimensional foreign policy and the future of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization

The article by Ahmet Sağlam, a Turkish international relations and business development specialist, in EU Reporter on Aug. 17 examines the evolving role of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) amid the Russia–Ukraine and Iran–US conflicts, highlighting Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic as key Central Asian actors whose multidimensional foreign policies and balanced relations with China, Russia, the EU, the US and the Turkic World can help keep the SCO focused on regional stability, economic cooperation and connectivity rather than becoming an anti-Western military bloc.

The article particularly emphasizes Kazakhstan’s role within Central Asia and the SCO, portraying it alongside Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic as an important balancing actor that maintains diversified partnerships across major geopolitical centers. Kazakhstan’s cooperation with China through the Belt and Road Initiative, security and economic ties with Russia, growing energy and investment cooperation with the European Union, and strategic engagement with the United States and the Organization of Turkic States are presented as part of a broader multi-layered balancing approach. The author argues that this multidimensional diplomacy strengthens Central Asia’s ability to maintain open communication between competing powers and could contribute to the SCO remaining an inclusive platform for dialogue, connectivity and economic cooperation rather than becoming a confrontational geopolitical or military bloc.

EU backs Middle Corridor expansion through South Caucasus

In August 2026, the European Union launched a new transport connectivity platform aimed at linking Europe with Central Asia through the Black Sea and the South Caucasus, reported Azernews on Aug. 18.

“According to the Europe-Caucasus-Asia Transport Corridor (TRACECA), EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that cargo volumes along the Trans-Caspian route could increase fivefold over the next 15 years.

Together with international financial institutions, the EU plans to mobilize approximately €2 billion for infrastructure development in the Black Sea region and the South Caucasus.

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are highlighted as the key participants in the development of the corridor.

Kazakhstan has invested $35 billion in transport infrastructure over the past seven years and has indicated that it plans to continue investing in the sector to strengthen its position as one of the key links between China and Europe,” reads the article.

World.title: Mid-August Weekend Full of Art, Music and Adrenaline
World.content:
ASTANA – From gallery openings and live music to high-octane drift shows, Astana and Almaty are heading into the weekend with a packed cultural and entertainment calendar. The Astana Times has rounded up some of the most interesting events worth stepping out for, whether you are looking for art, music, adrenaline or simply something different to do.

Astana

An exhibition dedicated to Leonardo da Vinci invites visitors to discover the artistic and scientific legacy of one of history’s most influential minds. Through reproductions, multimedia elements and interactive displays, the exhibition explores the inventor’s creative vision, engineering ideas and masterpieces, offering a closer look at the Renaissance era.

Venue: Palace of Peace and Reconciliation; 57 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.
